10534-the-double-traitor:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published this spy novel in 1915, opening at a fashionable Berlin restaurant. A woman dines alone with a young man newly removed from Paris, praising Berlin's Ritz-like rooms, flowers, soft carpets, and hidden orchestra. The scene sets a world of wealth, uniforms, and polite danger on the eve of war.

The young man, Norgate, finds Germany changed since boyhood, richer and more polished, yet full of secrets. Spies, double loyalties, and wartime plots will test him. Readers get a stylish, early thriller of Berlin society, love, and betrayal before the First World War.
1066-william-the-conqueror:
Edward A. Freeman, a Victorian historian, tells how William, Duke of Normandy, crossed the Channel in 1066, beat Harold at Hastings, and remade England. The book follows William from his rough youth as a bastard duke to his hard reign, with battles, castles, and the Domesday survey in between.

Freeman writes with a scholar's care and a storyteller's pace, judging Norman rule by its laws and its marks on the land. The conquest, in his view, joined England to Europe and changed its tongue and its laws. The book remains a solid short life of the king who remade a nation.
10842-the-life-of-captain-james-cook-the:
Arthur Kitson wrote The Life of Captain James Cook, the Circumnavigator, condensing his larger work into a popular edition with portrait and map. The preface, dated London 1912, promises nothing of importance omitted, with errors corrected and new matter on documents added. Chapters open with Cook's early years and his service in H.M.S. Eagle from 1755 to 1757.

The life follows Cook from Yorkshire lad to the navigator whose voyages mapped the Pacific. Kitson's telling is clear and admiring, made for general readers. The book remains a solid introduction to the explorer whose name marks coasts on three continents.
11105-jack-mason-the-old-sailor:
Theodore Thinker wrote this 1850 children's book about Jack Mason, an old sailor who has sailed almost all over the world and loves to tell stories. Jack, in a pea-jacket with a book in hand, talks to a boy sitting on a coil of rope aboard ship, and the boy lifts his head in wonder at each tale. Jack never swears, never drinks rum, and carries a Bible in his jacket pocket.

A fall from a high mast once hurt Jack's hip so badly that he stayed home a long time. Whale chases, dives for tin in deep water, and meetings with islanders fill the book. The tales teach courage, faith, and good conduct, in a sailor's plain, friendly voice.
1116-the-merry-wives-of-windsor:
Sir John Falstaff, short of cash, writes identical love letters to two respectable wives of Windsor, who compare notes and plot revenge. William Shakespeare's comedy follows their tricks: Falstaff stuffed in a laundry basket, dressed as a witch, and finally pinched by fairies in the park. The wives run the whole game.

The play, said to be written at Queen Elizabeth's request to show Falstaff in love, trades the history plays' wars for middle-class Windsor life. Its prose is brisk and its jokes are broad. The comedy still works as a farce of greed outwitted by quick wives.
11240-the-apartment-next-door:
William Johnston's 1919 mystery opens at three in the morning on Riverside Drive. where a young man in evening dress walks home and stumbles into a plot involving a face of hate, a card, a man called Mr. Fleck, and a sealed packet. Jane, the heroine, may alone know who the murderer is, and chapters follow clues in a book, a woman on a roof, a listening ear, and a house in the woods. The packet's contents close the book.

Johnston, author of The House of Whispers, writes a brisk detective melodrama in the postwar popular style. The apartment setting gives the mystery its claustrophobia: danger lives next door. Readers who enjoy period thrillers will find the plotting straightforward and the pace quick.
11252-martin-hewitt-investigator:
Arthur Morrison's 1894 collection introduces Martin Hewitt, a detective who rises from a solicitor's clerk after building an apparently impossible case, Bartley v. Bartley, out of nothing in the Probate Court. Seven cases follow: the Lenton Croft robberies, the loss of Sammy Crockett, Mr. Foggatt, the Dixon torpedo, the Quinton jewel affair, the Stanway cameo mystery, and the affair of the tortoise. Hewitt works by evidence and patience, not by flamboyant deduction.

Morrison created Hewitt as a deliberate contrast to Sherlock Holmes, an ordinary professional rather than a genius. The stories are compact, plausible, and grounded in London offices and homes. Detective-fiction readers will find Hewitt a quieter, workmanlike hero, and the collection a key document in the genre's early years.
12185-my-home-in-the-field-of-honor:
Frances Wilson Huard wrote this memoir of the First World War from her summer home near the Marne, about sixty miles from Paris. Published during the war, it records the weeks when a house party of artists and writers became a household under fire.

Huard describes the last peaceful days of July 1914, the sudden sight of soldiers on the roads, and the rush to shelter neighbors, bury valuables, and nurse the wounded. She writes of German occupation, evacuations at midnight, and the strain of keeping servants, animals, and guests fed. The memoir is personal, not strategic, and its power lies in small facts: bandages from old carpet, a trunk buried in a sand quarry, a village emptied overnight.
12314-ashton-kirk-investigator:
John T. McIntyre published Ashton-Kirk, Investigator in Philadelphia in 1910, with illustrations by Ralph L. Boyer. McIntyre, author of In the Dead of Night, created Ashton-Kirk as a thinking detective in the Holmes manner.

Pendleton calls on Ashton-Kirk, Miss Edyth Vale states her case, and portraits of General Wayne, a Schwartz-Michael bayonet, and newspapers playing their part drive the inquiry. A mid-book scene has the investigator pause on the street toward Spatola house, deciding to see the man himself first. McIntyre favors deduction and legwork over action. The novel is an early American detective story, fond of clues, interviews, and the slow tightening of a case.
13014-the-talking-deaf-man-a-method-prop:
John Conrade Amman, a Swiss doctor of physic, published this treatise at Amsterdam in 1692; it reached English in 1693 and London print in 1694. Amman dedicates it to his friend Peter Kolard and sets out a method by which a person born deaf may learn to speak. His claim rests on close study of how voice is made, not on signs or writing alone.

Amman explains voice as air made sonorous by trembling in the throat, skull, and bones, a tremor any reader can feel with a hand on the throat. He then maps each letter to tongue, teeth, lips, and nose, showing how m, n, and other sounds are formed by stopping or freeing the breath. The book is an early landmark in speech teaching, written when deafness was widely thought to bar speech for good.
1314-the-malefactor:
E. Phillips Oppenheim tells of Wingrave, a man cast out by society after a scandal, who returns from America rich and bent on revenge against the world that shunned him. The tale follows his plots through London drawing rooms, where love and hate tangle and his own heart betrays his plans.

Oppenheim writes the society thriller at a brisk clip, with disguises, secrets, and a final reckoning. The novel shows his gift for popular romance with a darker edge. It suits readers who like Edwardian thrillers of wealth, wrong, and return.
13239-grain-and-chaff-from-an-english-ma:
Arthur H. Savory's 1920 Grain and Chaff from an English Manor was published by Blackwell at Oxford. It recalls Aldington village, its manor house, and farm. Chapters cover the bailiff, hop foreman, head carter, shepherd, gardener, and laborers, then machinery, village politics, vicars, and school boards. Savory writes as a landowner who knew his folk by name.

He praises land girls in wartime, seventy or more in a camp under a lady captain. Yet he holds that strenuous farm work suits men best, while admiring one woman who digs with success. A garden couplet runs: a cherry year is a merry year, a plum year is a dumb year, explained by the small black merry cherry. The book is a warm, detailed portrait of English country life.
13274-a-little-catechism-with-little-ver:
Printed in London in 1692 for John Lawrence at the Angel in the Poultry, this little catechism gives short verses and sayings for little children. A catalogue of books follows, listing works on trade, clerical obedience, and family catechizing. The catechism itself is in question and answer form, meant to be learned by heart.

Children learn the commandments in order: no work on the Sabbath for man, maid, cattle, or stranger; honor father and mother; do not kill; do not commit adultery. Later questions ask how sins are seen: by searching Scripture, hearing preaching, examining conscience, and praying for God's spirit. A poor creature who comes to Christ, it says, finds arms spread wide open. The book is a tiny, earnest primer of old English piety.
13295-the-youth-of-the-great-elector:
L. Mühlbach's historical romance The Youth of the Great Elector, translated from German by Mary Stuart Smith in 1909, follows the young Frederick William of Brandenburg. Mühlbach, known for court romances of Joseph II, Frederick the Great, and Henry VIII, builds her tale in four books. Book one covers George William, Count Schwarzenberg, soldiers, diplomats, and revelations.

The young prince tells his tutor Leuchtmar he is discontented, since his teachers never forget the respect he once owed them. Later, a speaker knows every door of a castle on the Spree, including a little door never locked, hiding a secret door in a niche. The novel mixes court intrigue, love, and war, in the full-blooded style of Mühlbach's popular histories.
13311-three-articles-on-metaphor:
Three short essays from the Society for Pure English, published as Tract 11 in 1922, take metaphor apart with care. The writers are E. B., H. W. Fowler, and A. Clutton-Brock. Together they ask what a comparison should do for a reader, when it helps, and when it gets in the way of thought.

One essay states the test plainly: a good figure should leave no stray images to distract from the point. Another untangles supposed mixed metaphors in Parliamentary prose, showing that successive figures need not clash. The third warns against stale, ready-made phrases, from the lap of luxury to a sea of troubles, which say what others have said instead of what the writer means.
13498-the-fortieth-door:
Mary Hastings Bradley's 1920 romance The Fortieth Door opens with a rash promise and moves through masks, a pasha's palace, garden gates, and secrets of the sands. McLean, Tewfick, Aziza, and Miss Jeffries move through Cairo, bazaars, desert, and the tomb of a king, with a wedding present and a reception along the way.

Tewfick, pressed about a child's death long ago, recalls only that it came when his own daughter was very little. Later a woman plans escape, ready to thrust a gun into a prisoner's hands and follow him in a general's uniform for disguise. Bradley mixes Egyptian colour, intrigue, and love into a tale of doors, walls, and darkness passed through to light.
1361-tom-swift-and-his-giant-cannon-or-t:
Victor Appleton's boy inventor tale gives Tom Swift his biggest task yet: a giant cannon able to fire farther than any gun on earth. With his father, his friend Ned, and the giant Koku at his side, Tom plans the weapon, tests new powder, and races rival makers for a government trial.

Trials at Sandy Hook bring failures, a powerful blast, and at last a shot that breaks all records. The book mixes workshop detail with boyish daring and fair play. It is a brisk early example of the Tom Swift pattern: a bold idea, hard work, and a public test.
13832-romance-of-california-life-illustr:
John Habberton, author of Helen's Babies, gathered California stories in this 1880 volume. Tales include the schoolteacher at Bottle Flat, Jim Hockson's revenge, and the last Pike at Jagger's Bend. A new sheriff, a boarding-house romance, and old Twitchett's treasure add variety. The stories are thrilling, pathetic, and humorous by turns.

Habberton writes of miners, teachers, and small towns on the Pacific slope. A committee of Toledo men and miners waits on a schoolmarm to offer cordial support. Gold camps, saloons, and frontier justice frame the action. The humour stays warm rather than cruel. The book preserves early California local colour for modern readers.
13852-literary-taste-how-to-form-it-with:
Arnold Bennett published Literary Taste: How to Form It in 1913 as a practical guide. Chapters cover the aim, the reader's particular case, and why a classic is a classic. Bennett tells where to begin, how to read a classic, and how to wrestle with an author. Later chapters give system in reading, verse, and broad counsels.

Detailed lists build a complete library of English literature in three periods. Bennett warns beginners who see only words and miss the forest for the trees. He urges slow, steady reading over hurried skimming. Mental stocktaking closes the book. The guide suits new readers who want a plan, not just a list. It remains a friendly classic of reading advice.
14335-the-nursery-volume-17-no-101-may-1:
The Nursery for May 1875 is a monthly magazine for youngest readers, printed in Boston. It costs a dollar sixty a year, or fifteen cents a copy. Uncle Charles writes of a dog who lost his master, and Josephine Pollard of a child on a high horse. Emily Carter marks a grandmother's birthday, and George Cooper stages a doll baby show. The number speaks in short tales, verse, and pictures for small children.

One tale praises chickens wiser than Lottie, who stop to ask why while a hawk swoops. Mother Biddy faces the hawk so boldly that he changes his mind and waits for a safer chance. Another piece follows Dot, a small boy who lines up lemons while his father hides them behind his back. The family laughs as Dot finds the lemons in two rows. The magazine charms as a gentle primer in pluck, jokes, and kind hearts.
14425-mona-or-the-secret-of-a-royal-mirr:
Mrs. Georgie Sheldon's 1891 sensation novel introduces Mona, a beautiful young woman whose true identity is hidden behind a false name. The story opens in a Chicago hotel, where two gentlemen notice a fascinating young widow.

Mona takes work as a seamstress under the name Ruth Richards, enters the household of Mrs. Montague, and slowly uncovers secrets linking a royal mirror, a torn dress, and her own past. Sheldon piles disguise, eavesdropping, and sudden recognition into each chapter. The novel is brisk Victorian melodrama, written for readers who loved a mystery with a heroine at its center.
1456-an-episode-under-the-terror:
Balzac's short tale is set in Paris during the Reign of Terror, when an old nun and a priest in hiding seek shelter in a humble house. A stranger's kindness, a midnight mass, and a name from the past bind their fates to a man who once signed death warrants and now begs for mercy.

In a few pages the story turns on forgiveness, identity, and the strange mercy of revolution's victims. Its close is quiet and startling. It is one of Balzac's most moving miniatures, a tale of faith and guilt set in the darkest year of the French Revolution.
14882-bobby-of-the-labrador:
Dillon Wallace, author of The Lure of the Labrador Wild and The Wilderness Castaways, tells Bobby's story in Labrador, with illustrations by Frank E. Schoonover. Its dedication wishes a friend not gentle destiny or unearned bliss, but rugged trouble for a mate to mould the soul.

Bobby must learn a plain creed no man may fake. He must put the game itself beyond the score and take life's tide as it breaks, knowing the struggle a man should know before he can stand. Retreat, the book's frontispiece warns, may be hopelessly cut off. Wallace writes northern adventure as moral training: cold, work and courage shaping a boy into a man of the wild.
15003-draft-of-a-plan-for-beginning-anim:
Colonel William Wood drafts a plan for beginning animal sanctuaries in Labrador. It is for private circulation only, to be put to the fourth annual meeting of Canada's conservation board in 1913. A short summary opens the draft.

Wood recalls his original address, published in spring 1911, and a follow-up in summer 1912. This plan, a second follow-up, is now put forward for consideration. Papers are published for free distribution among those interested in preserving Labrador wildlife. Short and practical, the draft turns an appeal into a scheme: where sanctuaries should lie, how they should be guarded, and who should guard them.
15013-the-keeper-of-the-door:
Ethel M. Dell, author of The Way of an Eagle and The Knave of Diamonds, tells a romance of watching, waiting and a door kept shut. A lesson, an ally and an obstacle open the story, with the setting of a watch, a chaperon and a pain killer.

A puzzle, an elastic bond and a project follow, then the door itself, the impossible, a pal and her fate. A dark hour and an awakening lead to secrets. Published by arrangement with Putnam in 1915, in a fourth impression, the novel shows Dell at her most popular. It offers intense feeling, strong men and women, and love tested by duty, pride and a guarded threshold.
15157-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, this sixteenth volume of a fifty-five volume series covers the Philippines around 1609. It reprints early navigators' tales, island descriptions, and Catholic mission records, with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. A portrait of Morga's Sucesos fronts the volume.

Documents show political, economic, commercial, and religious life as Europeans first recorded it, from voyages to mission work. The editors add historical notes to place each text. Scholars use the series as a core source for Philippine history, and general readers can dip into vivid firsthand accounts of a far-flung colony.
1517-the-merry-wives-of-windsor:
Shakespeare's Windsor comedy follows Sir John Falstaff, who plots to seduce two merry wives, Mistress Page and Mistress Ford, for their husbands' money. The wives compare his identical love letters and turn the tables, ducking him in the Thames, beating him as a witch, and tormenting him in Windsor Forest.

Around the main plot, young lovers, a Welsh parson, a French doctor, and a jealous husband add farce and music. The play is broad, warm, and very English. It is Shakespeare's citizen comedy, written, legend says, because a queen wished to see Falstaff in love.
15412-the-virgin-birth-of-our-lord-a-pap:
B. W. Randolph, principal of Ely Theological College, read this paper before the Confraternity of the Holy Trinity at Cambridge, and Longmans published it in 1903. It is a piece of reasoned Anglican theology, written because debate over the Virgin Birth could no longer be put aside. Randolph treats the subject with care, aware of how sacred it is to believers.

His case starts from the Creeds, where two miracles stand at the center: the conception and birth of Christ, and the Resurrection. He argues that these two stand or fall together as the ground of Christian faith. The paper then answers doubts of his day and sets out why a believer should hold fast to the birth narratives. It serves as a short, plain defense for clergy and lay readers alike.
16048-troop-one-of-the-labrador:
A Labrador scout story by Dillon Wallace, author of tales of the far north. Troop One follows boy scouts in Labrador, where grit and a stout heart count for everything. The tale turns on a mystery: the shooting and robbery of Lem Horn. Wallace writes for boys who liked the outdoors and fair play.

Andy, a wonderful fine scout, goes out in the night when the weather is at its nastiest. His courage untangles the mystery, and the guilty are discovered and punished, as wrong-doers in time always are. The book closes on that plain moral, called the immutable law of God. It stands as a northern scout tale: cold, courage, and justice done.
16203-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume twenty-one of Blair and Robertson's Philippine Islands series, for the year 1624, turns to church affairs in the colony. Its documents cover ecclesiastical business from 1574 to 1624. A conflict between civil and religious authorities in Manila follows. A seminary for Japanese missionaries, an archbishop's letter to Felipe the Fourth, and royal orders on the religious complete the set. Early Recollect missions, told by Andres de San Nicolas, Luis de Jesus, and Juan de la Concepcion, run to 1624.

Facsimiles of title pages from their histories illustrate the volume, drawn from Edward E. Ayer's Chicago library. The papers show missions, authority, and empire tangled together. Students of Philippine church history will find a focused, documentary volume.
16305-crayon-and-character-truth-made-cl:
B. J. Griswold wrote this 1913 manual for teachers, parents, and Sunday school workers who wanted to teach with chalk. Each talk builds a picture in two steps, so the class watches a drawing grow while the lesson unfolds. The book gives the plan, the cheap gear needed, and plain steps for those who have never drawn in public.

Symbols run through the talks, but the stress falls on life and growth, not on fine art. A parent at home can use the same talks to teach a child both a simple skill and a moral point. The book is practical throughout, with notes on boards, paper, chalk, and how to hold a room's eyes.
16560-the-diving-bell-or-pearls-to-be-so:
Francis C. Woodworth, writing as Uncle Frank, offers children a book of short moral tales in this 1851 volume, with tinted pictures. The Name of My Book opens the set. The Scheming Spider, Genius in the Bud, Putting on Airs, The Fox and the Crab, The Greedy Fly, and Caroline and her kitten follow. The Wrong Way and The Right Way pair near the end.

Each piece is brief, with a plain lesson tucked inside a lively scene. Woodworth edited Woodworth's Youth's Cabinet and knew his young audience well. The book belongs to the gentle didactic tradition, charming rather than stern, and it still reads pleasantly aloud.
1667-my-aunt-margaret-s-mirror:
Walter Scott's My Aunt Margaret's Mirror comes from the Keepsake Annual of 1828. It opens with an introduction on the annuals themselves, miscellanies of prose and verse with engravings, put forth every year about Christmas. Aunt Margaret then tells a tale of a magic mirror that shows a lover's fate across the years.

Through the mirror's visions, a young woman watches love, marriage, and loss unfold, and the story weighs fancy against prudence. Scott's frame is leisurely and his tale is romantic. The story is a small Scott gem, best read at Christmas, when annuals were new.
16873-colony-or-free-state-dependence-or:
Alpheus H. Snow wrote this 1907 essay and address on what to call America's new island lands, issued in Washington. The essay is based on the political thought of the American Revolution, as summed in the Declaration of Independence. It asks whether the union's annexed regions are colonies, free states, dependencies, or just connections. It asks too whether the whole is an empire or a union. An address to the American Political Science Association at Providence in December 1906 sums the essay.

Snow argues from 1898, when Porto Rico and the Philippines came under a treaty with Spain that left their status vague. He weighs words as law, not just as labels. The book gives a clear, early legal view of empire's naming problem, useful for readers of American colonial history and of political thought.
1698-the-survivors-of-the-chancellor:
The Chancellor catches fire mid-Atlantic and breaks apart, and her passengers and crew take to a raft where thirst, hunger, and despair test every bond among them. Bound across the Atlantic, the Chancellor catches fire and breaks apart, leaving her passengers and crew adrift on a raft to face thirst, hunger, and despair, which test every bond among them.

Verne piles calamity on calamity with the care of a man working out a problem. Fire, storm, wreck, and the long wait for rescue each form a stage told through a journal kept on board. The book was called an imperishable epic of shipwreck. Its power lies less in any single horror than in the slow, exact account of how order frays when help does not come.
17040-the-survivor:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this novel of a survivor, fame, and revenge, in many chapters. Contents run from a sermon never preached and a strange betrothal into a man in a hurry and a lost address. A night in hell and next day, the author of No Man's Land, and an editor receiving a strange letter follow. A woman of whims and a first taste of fame appear. A visitor from Scotland Yard, Emily de Reuss telling a lie, and Joan Strong avenger lead to a tragic interruption.

Oppenheim mixes literary London, crime, and love, as Douglas Guest and Joan Strong chase fame, truth, and payback. The plot turns on letters, lies, and a past that will not stay buried. Readers who like Edwardian thrillers will find a long, plot-rich novel of ambition, guilt, and survival.
17460-lorna-doone-a-romance-of-exmoor:
R. D. Blackmore's romance of Exmoor, issued in this edition in 1889, stands among the best loved English novels of its kind. John Ridd, a Devon farmer's son, tells the story in his own voice. It runs from his boyhood on the edge of Exmoor to his love for Lorna Doone, a young woman held among the outlaw Doone clan in their wild valley. Farm life, moorland weather, and country custom fill the background.

The tale mixes adventure, feud, and courtship, as Ridd crosses the Doones, defends his home, and fights for Lorna's freedom. Its fame rests on the warmth of its narrator and the vividness of its West Country setting. Readers get a long, generous romance, often chosen as a first classic novel, where landscape and loyalty matter as much as plot.
17558-my-life-as-an-author:
Martin Farquhar Tupper, doctor of civil law and fellow of the Royal Society, published his autobiography in London in 1886 with Sampson Low, Marston, Searle, and Rivington. His Latin motto runs through the title page: I have lived, I live, I shall live. The contents open with a preliminary chapter, a sonnet, and a distinction between public life and private life, with Benjamin Franklin among the early subjects.

Tupper, once a best-selling poet of proverbial philosophy, looks back on his books, his public career, and his samples from his writings. Readers get a Victorian author's self-portrait, frank about fame and fond of his own work. The book appeals to readers of literary biography and of the curious career of a once-famous writer.
17870-operation-terror:
Murray Leinster's science fiction novel opens on a morning when radar picks up a strange thing out in space, and a man named Lockley wakes to a world about to change. The book came from the 1960s boom in space tales, when writers asked what Earth would do if a force from the stars chose to strike fear first.

Lockley, a calm, skilled man, must work out what the foe wants and how to fight back with weak tools and little time. Leinster keeps the science plain and the pace quick, with short scenes of dread, chase, and clever counter-moves. Readers who like tense, old-school space peril without long lectures will find this a brisk, fun read.
17887-the-green-door:
Mary E. Wilkins-Freeman wrote The Green Door in 1931, issued in New York by Dodd, Mead, with pictures by Mary R. Bassett. Letitia lives in the house where her grandmother and great-grandmother lived and died, kept by her very old, very bright great-aunt Peggy.

With no girls her age for a mile, Letitia plays grace-hoops, dominoes, checkers, and dolls with Aunt Peggy, while an old maid with a sore foot grumbles near. The tale turns on the green door itself, and what lies past it. Wilkins-Freeman writes with her usual plain grace, a gentle, late tale of childhood, home, and wonder.
17958-warlord-of-kor:
Terry Carr wrote Warlord of Kor as a science fiction tale of a dead world and the men who dig into its secrets. The cast list names Rynason, whose mind quest leads him too close to danger, Manning, whose colony plans leave no room for natives, and Malhomme, a ruffian preacher.

Horng, an alien of huge eyes and stiff mouth, tries to speak a tongue his race has not used for thirty thousand years. He warns that Kor is god and knowledge, and that humans must be stopped. Carr's tale asks whether Kor is legend, king, machine, or trap, and it ends as a tense, thoughtful story of first contact gone wrong.
18391-the-moravians-in-labrador:
A history of the Moravian mission in Labrador, first published in 1822, tells how the Brethren carried their faith to the Inuit of the far north. The volume opens with the Hudson's Bay Company settling among the Eskimo, and with J. C. Erhardt, who suggested a mission and wrote to the Moravian bishop. London merchants took up the scheme, engaged Erhardt, and saw it end in his death.

Jans Haven, backed by the British government, then sailed on a voyage of discovery, met the Inuit at Quirpont, and returned to England. A second expedition with Drachart and other missionaries followed, with talks, storms, an angekok's incantations, and efforts to keep peace between colonists and natives. Readers get a mission history from its own age: hardship, curiosity, kindness, and the slow work of conversion on a harsh coast.
18970-caves-of-terror:
Talbot Mundy wrote this 1924 tale of India, set around a hidden temple and a mysterious palace. A traveller hears wild talk of Yasmini, a woman said to rule hidden arts, command spirits, and keep a vast household behind guarded gates. Fear runs through every rumour about her.

The hero moves from city streets to caves, pools, and fire rites, seeking truth behind the tales of priests, mahatmas, and secret powers. Danger grows as wonder and dread mix in each new place. Readers get a fast, exotic tale of magic, faith, and courage in a land where no story quite agrees with the next.
1899-the-village-rector:
A woman named Madame Graslin carries a hidden crime into a French parish, and spends the rest of her life trying to pay for it with good works. The dedication to Hélène compares the book to a tiny boat launched under the protection of a revered name.

The story follows Graslin's work among the poor. Lawyers call her dealings a compounding of felony, and friends relate her troubles with amusement and pity. Balzac writes the provincial world with moral seriousness, and the novel's force lies in its heroine: a sinner who buys redemption with a lifetime of good works.
19140-girlhood-and-womanhood-the-story-o:
Sarah Tytler wrote this 1883 book of girls' and women's fortunes and misfortunes, in linked stories. It opens with Cain's Brand on a moor, moves to the stage at Bath, and follows Betty as nurse, Rowland to London, and girls travelling through Somerset. Each part tests character under hardship.

Polly, Lilias, Susan, Joanna, and Conny ride, bathe, eat peaches, and tease each other with schoolgirl talk, while duty and pleasure pull in turn. Their talk is bright and natural. Readers get Victorian tales for girls on work, family, and growing up, told with sympathy and moral care.
19142-the-devil-doctor:
Sax Rohmer wrote this 1916 volume of hitherto unpublished adventures of Dr. Fu-Manchu, called The Devil Doctor. Chapters include a midnight summons, Eltham vanishes, the wire jacket, the cry of a nighthawk, and the white peacock. The narrator, a doctor, follows Fu-Manchu's plots through London.

A false summons at one in the morning leads across a moon-bright common, where a French maid's charm and a false address at Rectory Grove raise suspicion. No living soul stirs, yet a warning voice speaks within. Readers get classic pulp villainy, exotic menace, and Edwardian detective thrills.
19340-the-story-of-the-big-front-door:
Mary F. Leonard wrote this 1898 children's story, The Story of the Big Front Door, with the motto that neighbours help one another. Children gather in cosy groups, tease about boys and girls, and watch a house across the street that looks camped in, with trampled grass and unknown damage. A front door bell calls them to tea.

Carl, Louise, Bess, Ikey, and little Helen trade jokes while Aunt Zelie keeps order, and guilty faces betray who trampled the garden. The Fords' tea bell relieves the strain. Young readers get a warm neighbourhood tale of play, mischief, and neighbours learning to help.
19671-the-annals-of-the-poor:
Legh Richmond, rector of Turvey, wrote these annals of the poor, published in London in the early nineteen hundreds. The best-known tale, The Dairyman's Daughter, traces grace at work in humble lives, where faith shines unencumbered by wealth or pride.

Later parts turn to sailors who go down to the sea in ships, see wonders in the deep, and cry to God in storm. Richmond's stories, long beloved in Sunday schools, honor poor Christians as full persons of spiritual depth. Richmond writes for Sunday readers, so each tale ends with a plain moral hope. In one home scene the dairyman himself comes in with two pails of milk on a yoke, having overheard his wife and daughter.
19926-standard-selections-a-collection-a:
Standard Selections collects and adapts superior readings for speakers and schools. One piece paints imperial Rome in the first century. It calls Rome the most revolting picture in history's pages. Society there rested on superior force and barbarous cruelty. Crime and mad profligacy complete the portrait. Such strong meat seasoned many school recitations. Pupils declaimed these passages in Friday exercises.

Elocution collections formed America's shared stock of quotable prose. Editors adapted long works into speakable extracts. History, oratory, and sacred writing filled their pages. A Roman horror piece taught both rhetoric and morals. The collection preserves what teachers counted as superior. It is a fossil of the recitation era.
19981-doctor-luke-of-the-labrador:
Norman Duncan wrote Doctor Luke of the Labrador in 1904. Islands off a cape shelter the harbor in its opening. They are great rocks, gray, ragged, and wet with fog and surf. The sea frets a thousand miles of rocky coast forever. Against that barren bleakness stands Doctor Luke's practice. The doctor serves fishing families scattered along the Labrador shore. Duncan knew that coast from reporting trips.

The doctor is modeled on Wilfred Grenfell, the famous Labrador missionary-physician. Duncan's novel made Grenfell's work known to thousands. Storms, ice, and distance are the practice's true partners. Each sick call becomes a small expedition by boat or dogsled. The book is adventure in service of portrait. It fixed Labrador in the popular imagination.
20358-jerry-junior:
Jean Webster published Jerry Junior in 1907, a companion tale of Jerry in Italy. A parrot chained to a perch watches over a vine-covered arbor. Morning coffee suits that shady spot, but afternoon tea does not. At close upon four on a July day, the heat rules all.

Gustavo emerges from the cool, dark doorway with his napkin floating. He scans the burning vista of tables and chairs before him. Webster sets young love amid Italian gardens, boats, and teasing talk. Readers get a sequel as light and witty as Jerry itself.
20462-ernest-linwood-or-the-inner-life-o:
Ernest Linwood, or The Inner Life of the Author is a novel that wears the dress of a confession. Its young hero looks back on his schooling and the people who formed him. Feelings run high, and small wounds leave long marks.

He remembers a tall, powerful man, his teacher, whom he had taken for a friend. The man might have spoken less harshly, the narrator thinks. He might have remembered the boy's youth and tender feelings before speaking so in front of others. The novel builds its tale of love and ambition on that inner life of pride, shame, and hope.
20544-the-little-skipper-a-son-of-a-sail:
G. Manville Fenn wrote The Little Skipper as a sea story for boys, about the son of a sailor. Fenn filled his books with ships, coasts, and practical seamanship. Here a young skipper and his sister Dot face the dangers of a working boat.

Trevor said nothing to Dot, the story notes, because there was no need. She was about the most prim, neat little creature that ever lived. She paced along by her brother's side carrying two sticks with iron hooks at their ends. Fenn's tales taught boys boat craft while keeping them turning pages.
20648-the-de-coverley-papers-from-the-sp:
The De Coverley Papers reprints the famous essays from The Spectator about Sir Roger de Coverley and his club. Addison and Steele invented Sir Roger, the kindly old Tory knight, in 1711. This edition, from J. M. Dent and Sons, gathers the papers in one small volume.

The preface borrows the Spectator's own words. To satisfy the curiosity natural to a reader, the paper designs itself and the next as introductions. It promises some account of the several persons engaged in the work. Sir Roger, the Widow, and the club members step forward again, in essays that defined English prose style.
20821-betty-wales-senior:
Betty Wales lands pink-cheeked and breathless on a station platform, curls flying wide. Margaret Warde seats her on a steamer trunk to fan herself with a tiny handkerchief. Rachel waits beside her as Harding College life resumes around them.

Senior year crowns the Betty Wales set of college tales for girls. Classes, friendships, pranks, and looming goodbyes fill this final volume. Warde, whose real name was Edith Kellogg Dunton, made college feel vivid and warm. Her books helped sell the dream of higher schooling to American girls at a time when few still went.
21042-roger-ingleton-minor:
Snow tables replace the old oaks of the park in Roger Ingleton, Minor. Gulls skim the dazzling down to the cliff edge, dingy against the white. Talbot Baines Reed paints that wintry coast as his tale of a minor opens.

A minor, a youth not yet of age, Roger faces claims on land and name. Guardians, rivals, and an old house's fate drive Reed's sober plot. Sea cliffs and snowy downs give the tale its stern, fair stage. Reed here writes less of school and more of duty, in a story of inheritance handled with his usual honour and pace.
21117-betty-trevor:
Mrs George de Horne Vaizey, who also wrote as Jessie Mansergh, set this novel in a London square. A family of boys and girls watches its neighbours there with keen interest. The children gradually get to know the households around them. Betty Trevor's family grows up inside that small, watchful world.

As the boys go off to interesting work, the girls turn to clothes, looks, and love. An undercurrent of old love affairs revived runs through the story to the last page, a Vaizey trademark. The square itself, loosely based on a real one, gives the novel its close, gossipy stage.
21248-the-little-colonel-maid-of-honor:
Annie Fellows Johnston's Little Colonel series, set in Kentucky, reaches its maid of honour volume in this instalment. It opens on a sunny May afternoon by the old sundial at Warwick Hall, where school work goes on quietly inside. The Little Colonel and her friends stand at the centre of another season of visits and ceremonies.

Johnston's list shows the series' reach: house parties, holidays, boarding school, Arizona, and a Christmas vacation, each volume selling at a dollar fifty. The books mix Southern settings, girl friendships, and family honour. This one prepares a wedding, with the Little Colonel in the title role beside the bride.
21281-the-colored-inventor:
Henry E. Baker was an assistant examiner at the United States Patent Office. He published The Colored Inventor as a record of fifty years since Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation. Writing in 1913, he argues that Black Americans should pause, review their progress, and take stock of the future the past discloses. Invention is his chosen measure.

Baker points to universities, schools, homes, businesses, and professions built since emancipation as proof of advance. His patent office post let him collect cases of Black inventors whose work official records often missed. The pamphlet asks that proper credit be given where it was earned, and preserves names that might otherwise have been lost.
21294-burr-junior:
George Manville Fenn tells this boarding school story through Burr himself, who arrives low-spirited in a bare, oak-panelled schoolroom of long desks. He quickly befriends Mercer, a boy weak at lessons but rich in natural history, which he shares with Burr and the reader. A gang of bullies makes their first days miserable.

Around the boys stand Hopley the gamekeeper, his daughter Polly, drill sergeant Lomax, poacher Magglin, and headmaster Dr Browne. Fenn, known for tales set in Malaya or South America, proves he can build the same tension inside one school. The last chapters turn properly nail-biting before the bullies and poachers are settled.
21530-the-angel-of-terror:
Edgar Wallace's thriller The Angel of Terror opens with a judge donning the black cap in a hushed court. First printed in May 1922, the book reached a thirty-second edition by 1934. The prisoner stands accused of shooting Ferdinand Bulford in cold jealousy.

Miss Briggerland's evidence says the man threatened Bulford and left her in a temper. By grim chance, Bulford stood outside his fiancée's door that night. Wallace, though unnamed on this title page, builds the tale from that verdict outward. A woman at the tale's heart earns the name of angel of terror, and lawyers and gunmen crowd the chase.
21617-that-affair-next-door:
Amelia Butterworth peeps through her curtains at a midnight carriage in Anna Katharine Green's That Affair Next Door. The house next door had stood in her view for years, quiet and known. On a warm September night, a carriage stops there, and her curiosity wakes.

Green, a founder of the detective novel, sets her spinster sleuth against Mr Gryce. The Van Burnam family fills the case: Silas, Howard, and the misses. Keys, order clerks, and reluctant witnesses crowd book one, called Miss Butterworth's Window. A labyrinth of windings forms book two. The tale, copyrighted in 1897, shows Green at her plotting best.
21637-the-dictator:
Justin McCarthy's The Dictator, reissued in 1895, opens with an exile in London. Paulo, the fallen leader, keeps a laurel in a blue pot on his balcony. It stands for honourable defeat that may yet turn to victory.

Chapters move through the Langleys, a gentleman-adventurer, and a soldier of fortune. Helena and Dolores draw the exile's heart in two directions. A Sicilian knife, a suppressed message, and an explosion raise the stakes. McCarthy, an Irish member of Parliament and a busy novelist, mixes politics and romance in a tale of a South American strongman's fall and hopes.
21638-tarrano-the-conqueror:
Ray Cummings pits Earth against a conqueror in Tarrano the Conqueror, copyrighted in 1930. A crowd of one hundred and fifty thousand hears the President at Park Sixty as the tale opens. The narrator stands on the tenth level, with twelve levels packed around.

Chapters promise new murders, a spy in the house, and flight to the North Pole. Georg escapes, is recaptured, and reaches Tara and the playground of Venus. A violet beam of death and waters of eternal peace mark the science of the tale. Cummings dedicated the book to Hugo Gernsback, champion of scientific fiction.
21870-luna-benamor:
A young Spanish consul waits at Gibraltar in Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's Luna Benamor, Englished by Isaac Goldberg in 1919. Luis Aguirre, consul at twenty-five, is bound for a post in Oceanica on his first great voyage. His family has served in diplomacy for a century, and doors open for his name. Gibraltar strikes him as incongruous and exotic, a mix of races and tongues under a foreign flag.

Around the title story, this volume gathers short tales: The Toad, Compassion, Luxury, Rabies, The Windfall, and The Last Lion. Blasco Ibáñez, author of The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, writes with heat and color. The Gibraltar of the tale, caught between Spain and the wider world, gives his consul a love and a lesson.
22136-the-book-hunter-a-new-edition-with:
John Hill Burton, a Scottish historian, wrote The Book-Hunter as a love letter to old books and their hunters. This edition adds a memoir of Burton and his own late revisions. Burton confesses he could not resist throwing in fresh touches here and there. He only hopes the changes do not spoil the book for its old friends.

The chapters wander through libraries, bookshops, auctions, and famous collections. Burton tells stories of rare finds, mad collectors, and books rescued from ruin. His humour is dry and his learning deep. The Book-Hunter has been a favourite of bibliophiles since 1862, and this edition shows the author still polishing his most personal work.
22327-development-of-the-digestive-canal:
Albert M. Reese studied how the American alligator's gut forms before hatching. His scientific paper traces the development of the digestive canal. Fifteen plates accompany the text, showing the stages under study.

Reese worked from embryos prepared with exact laboratory care. They were stained whole with Borax Carmine dye. On the slide, Lyon's Blue gave a second stain. Sections were cut across, lengthwise, and flat, at five to thirty microns thick. Thickness depended on the size of each embryo. Such detail makes the paper a record of early embryology at work. Anatomists can still follow his method and his findings stage by stage.
22366-the-church-and-the-barbarians-bein:
The Church and the Barbarians outlines the history of the church amid Rome's fall. It opens in the year 461, with the empire trembling into decay. That empire had ruled and united Europe for long ages.

The history of the empire toward Christianity is called remarkable. The imperial religion had been the deadly foe of Christ's religion. It fought that faith and, in time, was conquered by it. Then new peoples pressed in as Roman power failed. The outline follows the church through those centuries of invasion. Readers get a short, clear map of how faith survived an empire's collapse.
2237-the-merry-wives-of-windsor:
Sir John Falstaff, short of money, writes identical love letters to two respectable Windsor wives, hoping to profit from both. The Merry Wives of Windsor lets Mistress Ford and Mistress Page turn the tables. They lure the fat knight into a buck basket, a beating in disguise, and a midnight humiliation in the forest. Shakespeare's comedy runs on gossip, jealous husbands, and quick wives.

Around the main trickery swirl young lovers, a Welsh parson, and a French doctor, all chasing marriage and status. The town itself feels warm and lived in, full of taverns and households. Few comedies move faster or laugh harder at male vanity.
22540-the-k-factor:
The K Factor is a science fiction story about a science called Societics. Its founder had trained seven generations of students in its fundamentals. Then the creator himself defamed the article of their faith.

Hearing that defamation produced a negative feedback loop in Neel. The loop was so strong his hands vibrated in tune. It took a jarring effort to crack out of the cycle. Such language turns belief into machinery with loops and signals. A single factor, K, presumably holds the system's secret balance. Readers get idea-driven science fiction from the magazine era. Its drama comes from a science of society turned against its maker.
22546-the-reign-of-mary-tudor:
The Reign of Mary Tudor reconsiders England's Catholic queen and her record. Mary has long been remembered chiefly for persecuting Protestants. This history argues she was more inclined to mercy than most predecessors.

Stubbs speaks of her father's holocausts of victims, it notes pointedly. Persecution of Catholics under Edward was no less rigorous either. That persecution matched the persecution of Protestants under Mary herself. Her record compares favorably with Philip of Spain's rule too. His Council of Blood in the Netherlands outran her severity. Charles IX of France likewise fares worse in the comparison. Readers get a revisionist Victorian life of Bloody Mary. It asks fairness for a queen history treated harshly.
22745-fair-harbor:
Joseph C. Lincoln wrote Fair Harbor, a 1922 novel of Cape Cod life. Lincoln, the beloved chronicler of the Cape, filled his books with retired sea captains, small-town talk, and gentle humor. Fair Harbor returns to that world: a harbor town, its characters, and a captain whose sailing days are done.

The sample sits at a family table. The children eat in silence, as their mother taught them. Their father plays the part of horrible example. Macomber, too, is silent, busy stacking plates and cups for clearing away. Lincoln builds whole chapters from such tableaus, letting dialect and routine carry the comedy. Fair Harbor is a fair sample of his harbor: snug, funny, and salted with sea speech.
22757-debts-of-honor:
Mór Jókai wrote Debts of Honor, a novel by Hungary's most beloved storyteller, published in English in 1900. The catalog record names no author. Jókai's tales of Hungarian life mix family feeling, national history, and high romance, and this one opens in the warmth of a remembered household.

At that time, the narrator recalls, I was but ten years old, and my brother Lorand sixteen. Their mother was still young, their father no more than thirty-six, and their grandmother, some sixty years of age, had lovely thick hair as white as snow itself. From that circle the debts of honor, of love, money, and pride, begin to fall due. Jókai writes with his usual abundance of heart.
22835-the-london-visitor:
Mary Russell Mitford brings a guest down from town in The London Visitor, one of her village sketches. On Thursday, June 23, a note arrives from kind Mrs. Dunbar of the Hall. She begs the narrator and her father to dine that evening, since a London visitor has arrived without warning and the General is away.

The scramble to entertain becomes a small comedy of country manners. Neighbors rally, talk flows, and town polish meets village ease across the dinner table. Mitford builds the piece from observed detail rather than plot twists. Her sketches of Belford Regis life made her reputation, and this one shows why. Readers meet a whole social circle in a single evening's fuss.
22869-the-dark-door:
Harry Scott is running for his life in The Dark Door, a tale of pursuit and fear. Scott, thirty-two and in his prime, measures how far he has fallen. Months ago he set out on a quest he now calls ridiculous. Now men hunt him like game. Fear drives him on, helpless, certain of death unless some way out appears.

His hunters know too much, and there are too many of them. That imbalance powers the story, a chase told from inside the quarry's head. The dark door of the title promises the one way out, if Scott can reach it in time. The piece delivers pulp tension in a clean, direct style, built for readers who like the hunt more than the explanation.
23052-our-soldiers-gallant-deeds-of-the-:
Afghanistan's throne changes hands in Our Soldiers, a record of gallant deeds of the British Army during Victoria's reign. Shah Soojah fled Lahore in time and ended his days as a Company pensioner. Disorder gripped Afghanistan for years after his fall, until Dost Mahomed took Kabul's throne in 1826.

Campaign by campaign, the volume marches through the Queen's wars, India, Africa, and beyond, collecting acts of bravery for a proud home audience. Such books were the illustrated furniture of Victorian patriotism. Their facts are regimental, their judgments imperial, and both qualities now instruct. Readers get the British Army's own story of itself, told at the height of its confidence and reach.
23432-masterpieces-of-mystery-in-four-vo:
Joseph Lewis French edited this nineteen twenty two volume of mystic humorous stories, one of four volumes of masterpieces of mystery from Doubleday, Page. The editor thanks Brander Matthews of Columbia, Anna Katherine Green Rohlfs, and Cleveland Moffett for aid and for use of tales. He also thanks Arthur Reeve of Craig Kennedy fame, Wilbur Daniel Steele, and Ralph Adams Cram, among others.

Mystery here wears a lighter mask: strange doings told with wit, where the uncanny and the comic share the same room. Readers get a survey of the genre's playful side, from well known hands and lesser lights, chosen for charm as much as for chill. Fans of classic mystery will enjoy the mix, which shows that a puzzle can raise a smile as well as a shiver.
23606-the-man-next-door:
Emerson Hough, author of The Covered Wagon, wrote this nineteen seventeen novel of neighbours, town life, and ranch days, with pictures by Will Grefe. Chapters tell how the family came to move, where they threw in, how they lived in town, and how they spent Christmas Eve. The home ranch and better things follow.

A hired man, old man Wright's way of doing business, a fence dispute, and the talk of a daughter who never played for pikers fill the pages, in Hough's warm, western voice. Dedicated to the men with whom he rode in the old days, the book mixes humour, pride, and neighbourly strife. Readers who like western domestic tales will enjoy the family's move from ranch to town and the man next door who shapes their new life.
23847-the-peacock-and-parrot-on-their-to:
The Peacock and Parrot, on Their Tour to Discover the Author of The Peacock at Home, appeared in London in 1816, printed for J. Harris at the corner of St. Paul's. The little poem had been meant to follow The Peacock at Home at once. It was laid aside until its publisher judged it near enough in merit to that celebrated trifle to print with embellishments.

In verse, the peacock, delighting in noise and good cheer, determines for notoriety's sake to make a dash in the whirlpool of fashion. A concert and ball invite the beau-monde, and the birds fly off in pursuit of fame and of their author. It is a light Regency satire on fashion, poetry, and the hunger to be noticed.
24019-excelsior:
Bret Harte's Excelsior, presented by Enoch Morgan's Sons Company of New York, is a parody of Longfellow's Excelsior, turned into an advertisement for Sapolio soap. A youth passes through an Eastern village bearing a stencil-plate that reads complete: Sapolio.

The shades of night fall fast as he paints fences, oil cloths, floors, and wood work with Sapolio, beside Gargling Oil, Bixby's Blacking, and Mustang Liniment. An old man warns him off a fence spread with liniment, and he answers with a dash of paint. A maiden begs a rest from Bixby's Best and Simmons' Pills, and he answers only: will you try Sapolio. Beware the peaks, the poem warns, for that bright wall is but a snow bank, and paint will not stick.
24034-the-king-s-mirror:
Anthony Hope, author of The Prisoner of Zenda and Rupert of Hentzau, published The King's Mirror in New York in 1899. Its frontispiece carries the motto: I am not a king for my own pleasure. Hope, whose full name was Anthony Hope Hawkins, writes a novel of a king's education in power.

Chapters run from a pious hyperbole and a bird without wings to some secret opinions and two of my makers. Something about Victoria, a student of love affairs, and things not to be noticed lead to destiny in a pinafore and just what would happen. A political appointment, an act of abdication, and a king at a price follow, with pleasure taking leave to protest and the hair-dresser waiting. A chase of two phantoms, William Adolphus hitting the mark, and great promotion lead to the art of falling soft and the secret of the countess.
24134-mushrooms-on-the-moor:
F. W. Boreham wrote this book of short essays, published in a first American edition in New York in May 1919. It is arranged in three parts, and the title essay looks back to childhood mornings spent scouring dewy fields for mushrooms on the moor. The mushrooms themselves mattered little beside flushed cheeks, keen appetites, and boisterous fun.

Boreham takes such small, suggestive things, a corner cupboard, a wardrobe, onions, a baby's naming, and draws plain lessons for daily life from them. The essays mix memory, humor, and gentle moral thought. Readers get a warm set of reflections on how little moments can carry large meaning.
24376-floyd-grandon-s-honor:
Amanda M. Douglas wrote this novel, published by Lee and Shepard in Boston in 1899, copyrighted in 1883. It stands among the Douglas novels, from Bethia Wray's New Name, The Heir of Bradley House, and Osborne of Arrochar. Claudia, From Hand to Mouth, and Home Nook lead to Hope Mills, In Trust, and Whom Kathie Married.

The book is dedicated to Dr. and Mrs. Theo. R. Luff, in verse about friends far apart counting the loss and gain of vanished years. Its first chapter opens in high summer, early June, before the roses have lost their sweetness, at Grandon Park. Grand old trees and a bluff with strata of rock overlook a pretty settlement. A quaint house of rough gray stone, with tower, high balcony, and curious pointed roof, stands apart from Swiss villas below. Readers get a Douglas novel of home and honor.
24564-a-manual-of-the-operations-of-surg:
Joseph Bell, surgeon to the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, wrote this manual of the operations of surgery for senior students, house surgeons, and junior practitioners. The fifth edition, illustrated, sets out operative technique as Bell taught it in the wards and lecture rooms of Edinburgh.

Chapters take up operation after operation, with the instruments, incisions, and aftercare each requires. Bell, famous as a clinical teacher, writes with precision and practical sense. The manual remains a landmark of Victorian surgical teaching. It opens a window onto the operating theatre of its day, before modern anaesthesia, the drugs that block pain, and antisepsis, the cleaning that stops infection, had done their full work. Students learning their trade could study each step in plain, careful words.
2471-the-crusade-of-the-excelsior:
Bret Harte's Crusade of the Excelsior sends a shipload of Californians on a quixotic voyage, part pilgrimage and part gold rush dream. The novel follows the passengers of the Excelsior as their crusade meets reality: storms, rivalries, and the gap between lofty aims and human nature. Harte's humor softens the satire.

The book's California characters, transported to sea, give Harte fresh comic material. Its ending is bittersweet, as befits a tale of grand plans. Readers will find a late Harte novel of unusual scope. Harte published the novel in 1887, late in his California period.
25264-newfoundland-and-the-jingoes-an-ap:
John Fretwell's Newfoundland and the Jingoes, published in 1895, is an appeal to England's honor on behalf of Newfoundland. Fretwell argues that life as a crown colony is no partnership, since Britain sacrifices colonial interests to its own, while union with America would offer markets, protection, and hope.

His survey runs from Queen Elizabeth through Harley and Bolingbroke under Anne to George III's loss of America, which even Lord North disliked. Fretwell writes as a partisan for closer American ties, and the pamphlet preserves a frank colonial voice from the age of jingoism.
25419-polly-and-eleanor:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy returns to Pebbly Pit Ranch in this 1922 girls' adventure. Polly and Eleanor ride to Oak Creek to file a claim on a gold mine, then face claim-jumpers and a busy ranch household. Chapters take them to a beaver colony, a wild-west county fair, and Buffalo Park. They also form the Polly-Eleanor Company, Inc., and entertain guests with ranch hospitality.

The quieter thread follows Eleanor as she weighs an offer to attend school in a big city. Polly wants her friend to go, yet dreads losing her. A drive home in silence, with Eleanor dabbing Polly's tears, shows their bond. Grosset and Dunlap published the book, illustrated by H. S. Barbour, as a sequel to Polly of Pebbly Pit.
25459-the-cities-of-refuge-or-the-name-o:
Rev. John R. Macduff turns the Old Testament cities of refuge into a Sunday lesson for the young. His text is Numbers 35, where Moses appoints six cities for the manslayer fleeing vengeance. Macduff describes the roads kept in order, bridges over streams, and posts marked Refuge at every angle. Three cities stood east of Jordan and three west, so the nearest could be reached within half a day.

Provisions, wells, and Levite porters waited to welcome each fugitive into safety. Macduff draws the parallel plainly: parents, ministers, Bibles, churches, and good books are the modern refuge signals pointing to Jesus. Robert Carter and Brothers published the book in New York in 1865, from a sermon Macduff first preached to young hearers.
25595-a-queen-s-error:
Captain Henry Curties, author of The Blood Bond and The Queen's Gate Mystery, writes this 1911 adventure novel, published in London by F. V. White. He dedicates it to Sweet Kathleen of Bath, and chapter titles promise a breathless plot.

A strange visit opens the tale. A man with a glass eye follows, then arrest and torture. Cruft's folly, Sandringham, and the Duke of Rittersheim lead to a plot that failed. The ship Oceana, Don Juan d'Alta, a casket, and the Abbot of San Juan carry the chase on. A confession, a steel safe, an old graveyard, and a struggle in a tunnel close it before the queen's error and atonement.
25724-the-other-side-of-the-door:
Lucia Chamberlain, author of The Coast of Chance, writes this 1909 novel, illustrated by Herman Pfeifer and published by Grosset and Dunlap. A front picture shows the narrator looking up at a woman who, she feels, has won.

Contents open with a prologue on the city, always grey even in green March, then a basket of mushrooms, evidence, rumours, and days in court. A Spanish woman's house, a refuge, the last day of trial, concealment, and a light in the dark follow, with a lugger and an epilogue two years later closing a courtroom mystery.
25784-celebrated-travels-and-travellers-:
Jules Verne writes this second volume of Celebrated Travels and Travellers. Its subject is The Great Navigators of the Eighteenth Century. Sampson Low published it in London in 1880, translated from French. It holds ninety-six pictures and twenty maps. Hoisting signals for triangulation fronts the book.

A first volume, Exploration of the World, covered earlier history, and this volume follows eighteenth-century navigators who mapped oceans, coasts, and islands. Maps by Matthis and Morieu accompany pictures by Philippoteaux, Benett, and Matthis. Verne, famous for voyages extraordinaires, here turns historian, telling true voyages of discovery with the same sense of wonder he gave to fiction.
26380-complete-story-of-the-san-francisc:
The Complete Story of the San Francisco Horror, with an introduction by Rt. Rev. Samuel Fallows, gives a hurried, profusely illustrated account of the 1906 earthquake and fire. Richard Linthicum of the Chicago Chronicle wrote the main narrative, with Trumbull White adding twelve chapters on historic disasters. The quake struck without warning in the early morning, toppling great buildings, wrecking Stanford University, and breaking water mains so fire could finish the ruin.

Thousands died, tens of thousands lost food and shelter, martial law was declared, and relief ran to millions, with Congress voting funds. Eyewitness tales cover San Jose, where no brick building of two stories stood whole, and Agnew asylum, where floors fell in though walls stood. A Vesuvius eruption section follows. Two chapters end mid-sentence, a mark of hasty publication.
26512-description-of-a-new-vespertilioni:
J. A. Allen's 1897 paper, extracted from the Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History, describes a bat new to science from Yucatan. A small mammal collection sent by Dr. G. F. Gaumer from Izamal held a single specimen of Adelonycteris, apparently undescribed. Allen names it Adelonycteris gaumeri, for its collector, and gives the type as number 12753/11040, an adult female.

The description records dark brown fur above with an olivaceous wash, lighter buffy gray below, and black, naked ears and membranes with no whitish border. Measurements follow: length 95 millimeters, wingspan 286, wing 124, tail 40, forearm 39. The skull, about half the size of the related A. fusca, marks an old individual by its worn teeth.
26551-government-documents-in-small-libr:
Charles Wells Reeder, assistant reference librarian at Ohio State University, gave this address to Ohio librarians on October 8, 1909. It was reprinted from the report of the Ohio Board of Library Commissioners and printed at Springfield in 1910. Its subject is a practical puzzle: which government publications should a small library take, when it cannot take them all.

Reeder explains the depository system under the act of January 12, 1895, and the older congressional quota, by which members sent documents under their franks. He urges librarians to read their towns, taking farm bulletins for rural readers and debate material for high school pupils. Lists of useful serials, and how to get them free or by purchase, fill the rest.
26702-studies-in-love-and-in-terror:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes, Marie Adelaide Belloc Lowndes, published these five stories in 1913, reprinted here by Books for Libraries Press at Freeport, New York. The contents are Price of Admiralty, The Child, St. Catherine's Eve, The Woman from Purgatory, and Why They Married. Love and terror share the volume's title, and its opening tale sets the pattern of quiet domestic life shadowed by a secret.

Price of Admiralty opens with Claire de Wissant, wife of Jacques de Wissant, mayor of Falaise, standing on a wind-blown cliff path above the sea. She is great-granddaughter of the Trafalgar admiral who, both legs shattered by chain-shot, had himself placed in a barrel of bran to keep commanding to the end. A red-brick tower, a stairway down to a land-locked cove, and a bitter renunciation drive a story of marriage, memory, and the English across the water.
26885-the-looking-glass-for-the-mind-or-:
A sixteenth edition, printed at London in 1825, of this collection of little stories and interesting tales for young people, chiefly translated from Berquin's much admired L'Ami des Enfans. Seventy-four cuts, designed and engraved on wood by I. Bewick, illustrate the volume. A preface calls the book a collection of the beauties of Berquin rather than a literal abridged translation, with original thoughts and observations added along the way.

Virtue appears throughout as the wellspring of happiness, and vice as the root of every evil. No enchanted castles or supernatural agents appear, only scenes within the reach of young people in common life. Tales include Little Adolphus and Anabella's journey to market. They include Louisa's tenderness to birds in winter, Bertrand the poor labourer, and Nancy and her canary Cherry. They close with William and Thomas, or the contrast between industry and indolence.
26940-atalantis-major:
Daniel Defoe's Atalantis Major, first printed in 1711 and reissued here by the Augustan Reprint Society with an introduction by John J. Perry, is a political satire disguised as a tale of an island. Its England stands divided between Whigs and Tories, with the Sacheverell affair and the war still fresh in readers' minds.

Defoe writes as the Tories under Harley sweep the Whigs from power, backed by the Queen's open support. The satire maps parties, nobles, and councils onto island factions, giving modern readers a partisan's-eye view of Queen Anne's England at a moment of sharp political change.
27127-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume 26 of The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, covers the year 1636 in the great Blair and Robertson series of contemporaneous books and manuscripts. Edited and annotated by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, it shows the political, economic, and religious conditions of the islands.

Its documents include the nuns of St. Clare at Manila, a relation of 1635-36, and letters to Felipe IV from Sebastian Hurtado de Corcuera at Manila and Cavite. Hospitals and hospital contributions close the volume, with maps and views of Manila and Malacca among the illustrations. Edward Gaylord Bourne added a historical introduction and additional notes. The volume's illustrations include a map of the Molucca Islands.
27141-adenoids-what-they-are-how-to-reco:
Adenoids, number 2 in the Keep Well Series of the United States Public Health Service, was issued by the Treasury Department in 1919. The leaflet teaches parents what adenoids are, how to recognize them, and what to do for them, since about ten percent of all children have them.

Nature means us to breathe through the nose, where air is strained, warmed, and moistened. Adenoids are adenoid tissue, like tonsil tissue, grown abnormally large behind the palate, blocking free nasal breathing. The leaflet uses diagrams to show the blockage and its serious results.
27393-medal-of-honor:
Mack Reynolds wrote this science-fiction tale, illustrated by Bernklau, around an old tradition: a Galactic Medal of Honor holder could do no wrong. Captain Don Mathers, a one-man scout pilot, is about to learn in a strange way that the saying is true.

Mathers reports to his commodore after only five days out, explaining trouble in his fuel injectors on the third day. The commodore notes that this has happened four times in his last six patrols, yet the mechanics can find nothing wrong with his engines. Reynolds turns a routine report into a puzzle about duty, reputation, and what a medal really means.
27503-on-the-equator:
H. de W. published this Borneo travel narrative with Cassell, Petter, Galpin in London, and dedicated it to John Lancaster of Bilton Grange near Rugby. The journey runs out through Marseilles and Singapore to Kuching, on the Sarawak River, in the steamer Aline.

Later chapters give the history of Sarawak, Raja Brooke and Muda Hasim, rebellions, and the Chinese insurrection. They also describe Kuching society, the club, and the Sarawak Gazette, a climb of Matang Mountain, and travel up the Rejang among wild tribes. Kayan burials, head feasts, and tattooing appear in the account. It is a vivid Victorian travel book.
27966-the-dop-doctor:
Richard Dehan, author of Between Two Thieves and The Cost of Wings, published The Dop Doctor with William Heinemann in an edition, after a first printing and impressions through 1936. The dedication addresses one across the sea, with a long, melancholy reflection on years that brought bread and a roof rather than fame.

Dehan writes of quarrying bread and a home from the living rock with his pen, of hope's wings shed and love never sitting beside the hearth. The novel that follows is a Boer War romance of medicine, love, and empire, by a popular Edwardian storyteller.
28136-the-nursery-august-1877-vol-xxii-n:
The Nursery for August 1877, volume twenty-two, number two, is a Boston monthly for youngest readers. Its lead tale, A Day at the Beach, tells of two poor city children, Jane, nine, and her younger friend. They have seldom left brick walls and hot streets for green fields or shore. Other prose covers Buttercup and Daisy, a bullfinch, a poor man's well, and a dog named Tasso.

Verse includes a bumble-bee, King Drake, a cosset-calf, and Madam Quack, the last with music by Linda Cantoni. Drawing lessons and a picture-book note fill the rest. The issue mixes seaside joy with a kind look at city childhood.
28142-the-nursery-march-1878-vol-xxiii-n:
The Nursery for March 1878, volume twenty-three, number three, is a Boston monthly for youngest readers. Its verse opens with Nobody's Dog, a sad song of a black-and-white stray who follows strangers hoping to find a lost master. Prose covers a swing, boys helping their mother, a letter from Calcutta, prairie dogs, a catbird, and a boy who caught a fish with his nose.

Other tales treat a fly, grandpa's watch, Helen's bird, and geese with a hawk, closing with the snow country. Verse adds the new moon, a street-player, and the froggies' party, set to music. The issue blends pity for animals with home lessons and fun.
28143-the-nursery-april-1878-vol-xxiii-n:
The Nursery for April 1878, volume twenty-three, number four, is a Boston monthly for youngest readers. Its prose opens with Tired Out, in which Lily Macnish receives her first note, an invitation to a children's party. It goes on to Emma and a book, a bear and her cubs, and a monkey story. A deer tale and a drawing lesson add natural history.

Verse offers herons, Billy Brown sold, a bedtime song, and a trotting song, closing with a grasshopper lay set to music. The stories stress manners, kindness, and curiosity about animals. The issue shows the magazine near the end of its second decade, still aimed at the youngest readers.
28329-the-land-of-thor:
J. Ross Browne wrote The Land of Thor in 1867 as a travel book on Russia and the north, illustrated by himself. Browne, author of Yusef and Crusoe's Island, moves from St. Petersburg and Moscow to Revel and Helsingfors, with chapters on tea-drinking, markets, the Kremlin, and Russian manners. Harper and Brothers published the volume at two dollars.

Browne reports a bear hunt, a nose regiment, and a mysterious adventure, with notes on despotism, serfdom, and reform. His tone is curious and often comic. The book gives an American traveller's view of Russia in the age of Alexander II.
2835-the-canadian-dominion-a-chronicle-o:
Oscar Skelton wrote The Canadian Dominion for the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. He divides Canadian history after the French regime into three half centuries. The first fifty years after the Peace of Paris kept Canada separate from the United States under the British flag. The second period won self-government, and the third built a dominion.

Skelton follows governors, reformers, and councils through disputes such as Baldwin's demand in 1841 for French-Canadian members in the Executive Council. The narrative explains how responsible government grew out of such quarrels. The book gives American readers a clear short history of their northern neighbor, written before Canada's later constitutional changes.
28444-turn-about-eleanor:
Ethel M. Kelley's 1917 novel Turn About Eleanor begins when young David Bolling brings a small girl in a faded tam-o'-shanter to meet her aunts Beulah, Margaret, and Gertrude. The adults around Eleanor decide to try a cooperative experiment in bringing her up, sharing the work of parenting instead of leaving it to one person.

Chapters follow the experiment through Bohemian outings, a household of ten Hutchinsons, Christmas gatherings, and Eleanor's steady growing up, ending with a triple wedding. Kelley writes with humour and warmth about family rules, independence, and how children and grown-ups teach each other in turn.
28629-phoebe-junior:
Mrs. Oliphant's Phoebe, Junior, a Chronicle of Carlingford, centers on the daughter of the chief deacon of the Dissenting connection in Carlingford. Phoebe marries the Reverend Mr. Beecham shortly after his appointment to Salem Chapel, a match pleasing to her family but less so to other leading members. A substantial grocer with a paid pew seemed to some a safer son-in-law than a poor minister.

Chapters follow the pastor's progress, a leading member, Mr. Copperhead's ball, a country party, shopping, the Dorsets, and the Tozer family. Public meetings, a new chaplain, a domestic crisis, and a catastrophe test the chapel world. Readers get a sharp comedy of Nonconformist society.
28637-the-marriage-of-elinor:
Mrs. Oliphant's The Marriage of Elinor, published by the W. B. Conkey Company of Chicago in 1891, opens at a barrister's breakfast table. John Tatham, thirty-five, receives a letter asking whether he has heard of Elinor's new prospects, and whether he knows the man. The innocent question pales him, pushes his plate away, and spoils his tea and bacon.

Tatham insists the news is nothing to him, a thing he expected for four or five years, yet the letter shakes him. The novel then follows Elinor's marriage and its consequences, with family anxiety on every side. Readers get a Victorian study of pride, feeling, and a match made against advice.
2864-the-trumpet-major:
Thomas Hardy called The Trumpet-Major the most testimony-based tale in his Wessex series, drawing on spoken and written accounts of the Napoleonic wars. John Loveday, a soldier in the war against Bonaparte, and his brother Robert, a merchant seaman, both love the same woman in a Dorset village waiting for invasion. Hardy published the novel first in three volumes in 1880.

The book blends military camp life with village comedy, including a sailor's triumphant breakfast fry of eggs, ham, and kidneys carefully hidden under plate, coat, and hat. Love, rivalry, and duty pull the brothers apart and together. It remains a warm Hardy novel, less tragic than his later work and rich in Wessex detail.
28644-beyond-the-door:
Philip K. Dick's Beyond the Door asks what sort of lonely life a clock's bird might lead. The editor's note wonders whether such a bird could love and hate like any living creature. Larry Thomas buys a cuckoo clock for his wife Doris, without knowing the price he will pay.

At dinner Doris tears off ribbon and paper, crying out at a real old cuckoo clock like her mother's, from when Pete was still alive. Larry spoils the moment by noting Carl got it wholesale, and Doris flees clutching the clock. She winds it, sets its hands to two minutes of ten, and waits for the cuckoo. Readers get a brief fantasy of marriage, memory, and a bird behind a door.
28892-benefactor:
George H. Smith wrote this short science fiction story about Jacob Clark, an inventor whose robots have made him a target. A mob outside his door shouts down with Clark and death to the robot lovers, blaming his machines for unemployment. Clark tells his assistant Bill Towney that his inventions advanced the world a hundred years, and that he has always helped mankind, not destroyed it.

The magazine's introduction frames the question: robots will be fiercely resented at first, as an indestructible threat to workers, and their defenders will be called robot lovers and stoned. What happens next is the story's business. Readers get a short, sharp tale about progress, fear, and the inventor who cannot make the world love its own future.
29202-the-hammer-of-thor:
Charles Willard Diffin published this story in Astounding Stories in March 1932. Danny O'Rourke, stationed on a lone Sierra Nevada peak, has decided that the Director General of District Three, Ural Division of the Russian States, is a fool. An amazing incident at Stobolsk, the governmental headquarters, proves it to him.

Diffin pits Danny against a mysterious giant of space, in a clash the magazine compares to the hammer of Thor. The tale spans continents and stations, from a mountain observatory to a Russian headquarters. Readers get a pulp adventure of giants, governments, and a lone watcher who sees what his superiors miss.
3157-the-path-of-empire-a-chronicle-of-t:
Carl Russell Fish traces America's rise to world power in this chronicle. The Monroe Doctrine opens the story, followed by controversies with Great Britain, Alaska and its problems, and Blaine and Pan-Americanism. The United States and the Pacific, Venezuela, and the outbreak of war with Spain carry the narrative toward 1898.
