Dewey and Manila Bay, the blockade of Cuba, the preparation of the army, and the campaign of Santiago close the arc. Fish writes a clear, compact history for general readers, not a work of theory. It shows how a republic that began by warning Europe away ended the century fighting and holding ground far beyond its shores.
3249-the-major:
Ralph Connor names this novel for its hero, the Major, and opens on a coward. A fight for freedom, an escutcheon cleared, and salvage follow, with westward ho and Jane Brown. The girl of the wood lot, a voice in the wilderness, and the closing of a chapter mark the later course. The spirit of Canada and the shadow of war hang over all.

Men and a mine, a day in September, and an extraordinary nurse fill the middle passages. Hospitality without grudging and the tragedies of love test the hero's growth. Connor writes of a man remade by duty, from cowardice toward command. War sharpens rather than settles character here, and duty remakes a man the army first called a coward.
3401-the-elevator:
William Dean Howells sets this short farce in a smart hotel drawing room, where a dinner table gleams under low gaslight. Mr Roberts waits in evening dress, watch in hand, while his wife arranges her train on the carpet and worries that guests will arrive before the dinner is at its peak. The humor starts in that fuss over timing and appearance.

When visitors do arrive, polite talk covers awkward truths, and a small social machine runs on manners. Howells lets character show through dialogue alone, with no narrator to explain motives. The piece is brief, easy to stage in the mind, and a good sample of the light comedies Howells wrote about American city life.
3640-literary-taste-how-to-form-it-with-:
Arnold Bennett writes a practical guide to forming literary taste, with detailed advice on what to read and how to read it. He begins by clearing away a misconception. Many people treat literary taste as an elegant accomplishment, like good manners at a high dinner or skill on horseback, by which they hope to complete themselves for correct society. Bennett argues instead that taste grows from honest, steady reading.

The book lists classics, explains how to approach poetry, drama, and novels, and urges readers to keep notes and reread. Bennett writes for busy adults who feel ashamed of gaps in their reading. The guide suits readers who want a friendly, Edwardian path into serious books, without snobbery or academic jargon.
3687-the-ruby-of-kishmoor:
Howard Pyle writes a pirate adventure for young readers about the ruby of Kishmoor, a jewel famous for its size and color. The Rajah of Kishmoor had bestowed the ruby on his queen, and at her capture it fell into a pirate's hands. A prologue introduces a very famous pirate of his day, and chapters follow Jonathan Rugg, a mysterious lady with a silver veil, and a one eyed little gentleman in black.

Later adventures bring a stranger with silver earrings and a sea captain with a broken nose, all chasing the great stone. Pyle writes with the gusto of a storyteller who loved ships, swords, and treasure. The book suits young readers who enjoy classic pirate tales with humor and high color.
371-literary-blunders-a-chapter-in-the-h:
Henry Wheatley catalogs the slips, ghosts, and false tales of bookish life in this amusing study. He takes his title from a jest in The Caxtons, where a grand History of Human Error never got past its first sheets. Wheatley then sorts real blunders by kind, from bad quotes to fake authors and phantom words.

Chapters treat authors, translators, book lists, and errata sheets, with tales of learned men caught out by their own print. Ghost words coined by misreading get a full airing. The book delights readers who love books, and it warns how fast one error in print can live for years.
3808-robur-the-conqueror:
Jules Verne launches Robur the Conqueror with a duel that misses both men and a cow, then lifts the tale into the sky. The Weldon Institute of Philadelphia, devoted to balloons, faces a visitor who scorns gas bags and promises a heavier than air flying machine. Soon its president Uncle Prudent and secretary Phil Evans wake as prisoners aboard the Albatross, a great aeronef with a golden sun on its flag.

The voyage sweeps across prairies, the Pacific, the Himalayas, the Caspian, Dahomey, and the Atlantic, while the captives shout their names in vain to cheering crowds below. The balloon Go-Ahead rises to challenge Robur and collapses in the attempt. Readers who like Verne's inventor tales will find a swift tour of the world from above, with a villain who flies beyond all law.
412-john-jacob-astor:
Elbert Hubbard profiles John Jacob Astor in this Little Journeys sketch of great business men. Hubbard opens with Astor's plain habits: early rising, steady work, and a life ruled by routine rather than luck. Wealth, he argues, follows habit, service, and the will to give value in return.

The sketch traces Astor from a poor German youth to the fur trade and New York land, where patience built a fortune. Hubbard writes in brisk, moralizing prose, full of maxims on work and thrift. The piece serves as both life and lesson, in the self-help style that made Hubbard's series popular.
4266-a-woman-s-way-through-unknown-labra:
Mina Benson Hubbard wrote this book to complete her husband Leonidas Hubbard's unfinished work in Labrador. She wanted to correct misleading accounts of his expedition. She includes much of his diary exactly as he wrote it. She adds George Elson's account of their last days together and his later efforts. A map of the region is included.

Her own journey crossed country recognized by geographical authorities in America and Europe. It was the only surveyed route over that region. The narrative moves through rivers, lakes, and portages, with the daily labor of travel. It stands as a tribute to her husband and a record of a woman leading an expedition through unknown land.
4343-how-and-when-to-be-your-own-doctor:
Dr. Isabelle A. Moser, with Steve Solomon, wrote this guide to natural hygiene and self-care, published in 1997. Its chapters tell how Moser became a hygienist, explain the nature and cause of disease, and cover fasting, colon cleansing, diet and nutrition, vitamins, and the analysis of disease states.

The book argues that the body recovers when given rest, clean food, and freedom from excess, and it teaches readers to help that process. Solomon's foreword sets the tone with a Shaker hymn on the gift of simplicity. Readers should note that its advice is alternative health teaching, not a substitute for medical care.
4624-off-hand-sketches-a-little-dashed-w:
T. S. Arthur published Off-Hand Sketches, a little dashed with humour, in 1851. He notes that readers will smile at some slices of life pictured here, yet no smile here is bought by slighting humanity, good feeling, or virtue. Most episodes are true stories given a light imaginative colouring, and each carries a lesson worth taking to heart.

Contents include the circuit-preacher, the protest, and retrenchment, or what a man saved by stopping his newspaper. They go on to hunting up a testimonial, trying to be a gentleman, taking a prescription, and the Yankee and the Dutchman. Later sketches cover a tipsy parson, much ado about Mrs. Todd and Mrs. Jones, almost a tragedy, a new way to collect an old debt, and a shocking bad memory. Readers get short, funny, moral American sketches.
471-the-bride-of-lammermoor:
Walter Scott tells a tragic Scots romance of feuding houses in this novel. Edgar, Master of Ravenswood, loves Lucy Ashton, daughter of the man who seized his family's lands. Their secret betrothal defies kin, law, and a mother's cold scheming, and the tale moves toward a grim, fated end.

Scott frames the story as drawn from a real Dalrymple family tale, told to him by kin near the events. Moor, castle, and storm set the dark ground. The novel endures as Scott's starkest tragedy, where love, pride, and revenge pull young lives toward ruin.
4945-jane-allen-junior:
Edith Bancroft's Jane Allen: Junior opens on a late September day at Wellington College, where summer waves goodbye with fitful sunshine through stately trees. Leaves tremble before autumn's brush, buds burst in heroic tribute, and breezes cheer the pageant of farewell.

Jane and her friend Norma Travers face a new school year, with classes, friendships, and the small dramas of college life ahead. Bancroft writes in the girls' school-story tradition, warm and detailed about campus routine. Readers get a gentle college novel about growing up among friends, told in the season's turning light.
5003-the-rover-boys-in-new-york-or-savin:
Arthur M. Winfield's Rover Boys in New York opens with the brothers planning a sail in the Dartaway, teasing Dick about visiting Dora at Hope Seminary and Tom about his dread of another storm. Sam, Tom, and Dick Rover banter like brothers who have shared many scrapes before.

The New York trip soon turns serious, as the boys work to save their father's honor against charges that threaten the family name. Boating, city adventure, and school loyalty mix in the usual Rover fashion. Readers get a boys' series tale where fun comes first, but family duty gives the adventure its stakes.
5054-the-dream-doctor:
Arthur B. Reeve's Dream Doctor follows Professor Craig Kennedy through cases introduced by his friend Jameson, a Star reporter summoned by his managing editor. The editor, sorting letters on his desk, reads one from a Constant Reader asking whether Professor Kennedy is really all the stories claim, and sends Jameson to get the real story.

Cases follow on a coke fiend, a submarine mystery, a wireless detector, ghouls, X-ray movies, and a death house, ending on a final day. Reeve's scientific detective uses new technology as his magnifying glass. Readers get early forensic fiction, where dreams themselves become evidence and the laboratory solves the crime.
5065-civil-government-for-common-schools:
This manual of civil government for common schools argues that textbooks fail pupils by stopping with theory. Students learn the science of government and the guaranty of republican rule. They do not learn how government works in their own town. They do not learn what causes a justice of the peace can try, or how a school district actually works.

To fill that gap, the manual begins with the school district. It proceeds through town, county, and state practice. It joins theory to the art of government as practiced locally. The work is cataloged without an author. Teachers and students get a practical civics book, written to make government visible in the places where pupils actually live.
5073-the-war-terror:
Arthur B. Reeve's War Terror gathers Craig Kennedy cases for a nation at war. Chapters cover an electro-magnetic gun and a murder syndicate. An air pirate, an ultra-violet ray, a triple mirror, and wireless wiretappers follow. A houseboat mystery, a radio detective, a curio shop, and a pillar of death come next. Arrow poison, a radium robber, and a spinthariscope add to the set.

Later cases add an asphyxiating safe, a dead line, a paste replica, a burglar's microphone, a germ letter, and an artificial kidney. Reeve's scientific detective meets wartime invention at every turn. Readers get pulp science detection at its most inventive, where each new device becomes both weapon and clue.
5118-the-american-senator:
Anthony Trollope's novel, first serialised in 1876 and published in book form in 1877, brings an American senator to the English village of Dillsborough. His blunt questions about English customs, law, and land stir up the local families, especially the Mortons and the Masters, and expose the habits of a small rural community.

Around the visitor's tour, Trollope weaves courtship, family pride, and a dispute over poaching and property. The book works as both a comedy of manners and a comparison of two nations, with the senator's outsider eye sharpening every clash between old English ways and new American plain speaking.
5317-through-the-magic-door:
Arthur Conan Doyle's Through the Magic Door invites readers to shut the door of their room, leave the cares of the outer world behind. Readers plunge into the company of the great dead. However humble the bookshelf, Doyle says, its noble, silent comrades wait in ranks. Choosing a man from their files carries the reader through a magic portal.

The book's twelve chapters are essays on books and authors, written by the creator of Sherlock Holmes as a lover of reading. Readers will find a warm, personal guide to literature, in which Doyle shares his enthusiasms. It argues that books offer a fair land where worry cannot follow.
5332-the-love-sonnets-of-a-car-conductor:
Wallace Irwin's Love Sonnets of a Car Conductor parodies the sonnet in streetcar slang. It carries a harmless and instructive introduction by the fictional Professor Wolfgang Copernicus Addleburger of the University of Monte Carlo. Irwin, author of The Love Sonnets of a Hoodlum, gives his conductor a muse and a route, and lets him sing of love in the language of the car.

The introduction, by a scientist who reaches the transcendental by winding paths, sets the joke in motion. Readers get a light, comic volume of dialect verse, in which high poetic form meets low city life, and both come out laughing.
5333-every-man-in-his-humor:
Ben Jonson's Every Man in His Humor, in its Anglicized edition, is the comedy that first made Jonson's name. The introduction presents Jonson as the greatest English dramatist after Shakespeare, a commanding figure and poet laureate whose strong personality shaped the course of English letters.

Jonson, grandson of a man from Annandale by the Solway, sets his comedy in London, where each character is ruled by a humour, a ruling passion or folly. Readers will find a lively, satiric portrait of Elizabethan city life, with young gallants, merchants, and soldiers, all acting exactly in their humour.
6108-boy-scouts-in-a-submarine-or-search:
G. Harvey Ralphson sends the Boy Scouts into a submarine to search an ocean floor, opening in the handsome, noisy clubroom of the Black Bear Patrol in New York, ablaze with light. The Sea Lion proves equal to her task, and through the night a chase goes on.

Chapters promise a dandy submarine, a wolf on the trail, two wolves in a pen, night on an ocean floor, the secret of the hold, and guard duty under the sea. Jimmie goes hunting, Jack makes a discovery, and a desperate prisoner and a bluff that didn't work follow. Ralphson mixes scout pluck with undersea adventure.
6313-masterpieces-of-american-wit-and-hu:
Thomas L. Masson edits this fourth volume of American wit and humor, with Mark Twain pictured at the front and a roster running from Agnes Repplier to Harriet Beecher Stowe. Repplier pleads for humor, Marietta Holley writes an unmarried female, and Fitzhugh Ludlow offers selections from a brace of boys. Robert Jones Burdette cures rheumatism by movement, Oliver Wendell Holmes gives an aphorism and a lecture, and Artemus Ward writes business letters.

James Russell Lowell, Louisa May Alcott on Washington street scenes, and Samuel Minturn Peck join William Cullen Bryant on the mosquito and Danforth Marble on the Hoosier and the salt pile. The 1903 collection mixes essays, sketches, and verse, light in touch and broad in range. It is a sampler of a nation's funny bone, from parlour satire to frontier tall talk.
6482-the-coverley-papers-from-the-specta:
O. M. Myers edits The Coverley Papers from the Spectator, gathering every number concerned with Sir Roger de Coverley or arising from the Spectator's visit to his country house. Sir Roger appears in some seventeen other papers, but there he gets only passing mention or speaks where the subject, not he, is the interest. The contents list Addison, Steele, and Budgell numbers across the Spectator's run, with appendices on coffee houses, the Spectator's acquaintance, and Sir Roger's death.

Myers's introduction urges studying Addison in close relation to his time, for he was a true child of his century, not so much in opposition to it. A mid passage contrasts neighbours Laertes and Irus, whose ways of living are an abomination to each other. Laertes charges his estate yearly with a child's birth rather than let a new man equal him. The papers are Augustan comedy, gentle and observant.
6802-white-slaves-or-the-oppression-of-t:
Louis Albert Banks, dedicating his book to parents who taught him love of liberty and hatred of oppression, writes on white slaves, the oppression of the worthy poor. He opens with Edison's note that ninety percent of coal's energy is lost in turning it to force, and asks if nearly as much spiritual power is wasted in average church life. Fervor in meetings, he notes, yields meagre results.

Banks, a Methodist preacher, urges churches to aid the poor in deed, not just in devotion. His tone is earnest, reforming, and plain. White Slaves is a passionate, period plea for social justice from a pulpit voice.
6837-the-little-warrior:
Wodehouse opens The Little Warrior with Freddie Rooke gazing coldly at breakfast, eye-glass gleaming, at a poached egg Parker has placed before him. What is this, Freddie asks in pain; poached egg, sir, Parker replies. It looks just like an old aunt of mine, Freddie says, and orders it removed, then stands by the fireplace in his dressing-gown, shoulders to the mantel.

From that comic breakfast grows a tale of love, golf, and a little warrior's battles in London and New York. Wodehouse keeps the farce light and the dialogue crisp. The Little Warrior is a gay, classic Wodehouse novel, full of silly young men and sensible girls.
6934-the-radio-amateur-s-hand-book-a-com:
This handbook teaches the amateur how to receive and send messages without wires, from first set to working station. Its author, A Frederick Collins, won a gold medal for his wireless telephone at the Alaska Yukon Pacific Exposition in 1909. The book covers both wireless telegraphy and telephony, with numbered figures that match the text figure for figure.

Readers learn the parts, the circuits, and the practice of tuning, calling, and answering across the air. The opening pages sketch how the art grew and where it is used in daily life, so a beginner grasps the why before the how. It is a hands on manual for the 1920s listener turned builder, plain in speech and rich in diagrams.
6935-the-radio-amateur-s-hand-book-a-com:
A Frederick Collins, inventor of the wireless telephone in 1899, wrote this handbook for radio amateurs in 1922. Dedicated to William Marconi, inventor of the wireless telegraph, it claims to be a complete, authentic, and informative work on wireless telegraphy and telephony. Collins had already written on wireless telegraphy in 1905 and served as historian of wireless from 1901 to 1910.

The introduction promises first a word on the history of the art and its present day uses, before turning to the mysteries of sending and receiving messages without wires. Illustrations are keyed to the text by number, so a reader can follow each set and circuit. The book speaks to the early amateur eager to build, listen, and talk across the air.
7191-modern-broods-or-developments-unloo:
Charlotte Mary Yonge's 1900 novel takes its motto from Tennyson: youth and age are scholars yet but in the lower school. Its chapters move from tortoises and hares through the Goyle, a first Sunday, and cycles. Clipstone friends, frescoes of St Kenelm, sisters, and snobbishness trace how a younger brood grows in ways their elders did not foresee.

Yonge watches family life with a moral eye, letting small choices, church Sundays, and social slights reveal character. The title's unlooked-for developments give the book its mild comedy and its sting, as parents find their children turning out unlike their plans. The novel stays close to home, where its quiet drama feels most true.
7529-the-reverberator:
Henry James's novella opens in a Paris hotel's little reading room, where an old man leads a visitor to his daughter. The room holds a window with much curtain and no light, a Figaro the visitor cannot read, and a New York Herald he has already read. The visitor is George Flack, an American journalist of characteristic directness, and the girl is Francina Dosson, traveling with her father.

Flack's trade is the story, and the novella's comedy and sting come from what happens when private talk reverberates into print. Paris society, American innocence, and the press collide, as a young woman's reputation travels faster than she can control it. The Reverberator is James on journalism and gossip, witty, sharp, and quietly sad.
8106-captain-cook-s-journal-during-his-f:
Captain James Cook's journal of his first voyage round the world in HMS Bark Endeavour, 1768 to 1771, appears here in a literal transcription of the original manuscripts, edited by Captain W. J. L. Wharton, hydrographer of the Admiralty, and published in London in 1893. The volume includes maps, facsimiles, and a portrait with Cook's signature, and is dedicated to the Duke of Edinburgh for his interest in the British navy.

The journal records the voyage to Tahiti for the transit of Venus, the charting of New Zealand, and the east coast of Australia, day by day, in Cook's plain seaman's prose. It is the primary source for one of history's great voyages. For readers of exploration, it offers the Pacific as Cook himself saw it, without later romance.
840-lorna-doone-a-romance-of-exmoor:
R. D. Blackmore wrote this romance of Exmoor, where John Ridd, a sturdy Devon farmer, loves Lorna Doone, a maiden of the outlaw clan that haunts the moors. Blackmore calls it a romance, not a history, for its scenes, folk, and times are alike romantic. The tale moves from farm to moor, from love to feud and battle.

John's plain voice carries the story, with humour, dialect, and a love of the land. The Doones, fierce and proud, stand against law and neighbours, and Lorna's fate hangs on the feud. The novel has lasted as a classic English romance, beloved for its heroine, its villain clan, and its wild Exmoor setting.
8550-t-haviland-hicks-senior:
J. Raymond Elderdice wrote T. Haviland Hicks, Senior, for schoolboys, dedicating it to Master Lloyd Elderdice. Contents promise Hicks, wild west bad man, Leave It to Hicks, and Hicks's prodigious prodigy. A letter from Scoop Sawyer follows, with Hicks making a decision, making a speech, starting another mystery, Coach Corridan surprising the eleven, and Theophilus in further adventures.

Hicks, the senior boy, leads school stories in the classic pattern: sports, scrapes, and a wild west reputation tamed by school life. Readers of boys' fiction get a brisk, old-fashioned tale, where a school hero sorts out mysteries and teams alike. The book suits young readers and collectors of school stories.
8578-the-grand-inquisitor:
Feodor Dostoevsky's famous chapter, taken from The Brothers Karamazov, imagines Christ returning to Seville during the Inquisition and being arrested by the Grand Inquisitor. In H. P. Blavatsky's translation, the old churchman argues that people cannot bear freedom, and will trade it for bread, authority, and miracle. Christ answers with silence, and at the end kisses the Inquisitor on the lips.

The passage stands alone as a fierce debate about faith, power, and human nature, which is why it is so often printed apart from the novel. Dostoevsky, then newly dead when this version appeared, uses the scene to press his deepest question: whether love can survive without force. Readers new to Russian fiction can start here and feel the novelist's full weight in a single short episode.
8729-the-dancing-mouse-a-study-in-animal:
Robert M. Yerkes, instructor in comparative psychology at Harvard, studies the dancing mouse in this first volume of the Animal Behavior Series. The book, dated 1907, grew from an essay that won the Cartwright Prize of the Columbia physicians and surgeons alumni in 1907, comprising its first twelve chapters. Yerkes dedicates it in love and gratitude to his mother, and opens with the mouse's characteristics, origin, and history, its markings and its method of keeping.

Dancing mice spin, circle, and sniff in patterns that made them favourites of fanciers and puzzles for psychologists. Yerkes tests their senses, learning, and behaviour with careful experiments, founding a field that would grow into modern animal psychology. The book remains a landmark of early behaviour study, readable for its clear methods and its affection for its small, whirling subjects, even where later science has moved beyond it.
8931-the-gem-collector:
P. G. Wodehouse published The Gem Collector in Ainslee's Magazine in December 1909. Later revised and republished in 1910 as The Intrusion of Jimmy, also known as A Gentleman of Leisure. A transcriber's note explains that the magazine version had two chapters headed chapter eighteen and ended with chapter nineteen, now relabelled nineteen and twenty. That one word in chapter six has been corrected from pubrescent to putrescent. The story opens in the Savoy Hotel supper room, all brightness and glitter and gaiety.

Sir James Willoughby Pitt, baronet, looks round through cigarette smoke and moodily judges the world flat, despite the geographers. From that bored aristocrat, Wodehouse builds a comedy of jewel theft, imposture, and romance in high society and country houses. Readers who know Wodehouse from Jeeves will recognize the early, breezier voice, and a hero who steals, charms, and reforms himself in the same breath.
9087-eleanor:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote this novel in 1900 and dedicated it to Italy, called here the instructress of the past and delight of the present. Its heroine, Eleanor, lives among English folk in Italy, where love, duty, and faith pull her in hard directions. A young visitor, Lucy Foster, and a priest, Father Benecke, shape the tale's turns.

Ward sets English reserve against Italian warmth, and lets her characters argue out questions of marriage, belief, and the claims of the heart. The prose is earnest and rich in place detail, from villas to loggias. Eleanor remains a good sample of the serious society novel at the turn of the century.
9097-robert-s-rules-of-order-pocket-manu:
Major Henry M. Robert, an officer in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, wrote this pocket manual in 1876 and printed it in Chicago. It sets out parliamentary law based on the rules and practice of Congress, but fitted to ordinary societies, conventions, and clubs. Part one gives rules of order; part two tells how to run a meeting.

For each motion Robert states its aim, its effect, and whether it can be changed or debated, in a set order any chair can follow. The book filled a real need, and it grew into the standard guide still used in meetings today. This first edition shows the system at its plain, practical start.
923-a-sketch-of-the-life-of-brig-gen-fra:
William Dobein James wrote this sketch of Brigadier General Francis Marion and a history of his brigade, from its rise in June 1780 until it disbanded in December 1782. The book adds descriptions of characters and scenes not before published, and an appendix with copies of letters from Marion's own hand.

James, who served with Marion's men, tells of swamp raids, skirmishes, and the hard life of partisans in South Carolina. His account is first-hand, plain, and full of local detail. The volume is a prime source for the Southern war, valued by historians for its eyewitness voice and its documentary appendix.
9457-travels-in-arabia-comprehending-an-:
John Lewis Burckhardt, who died before publication, wrote these travels in Arabia, issued in London in 1829 by the Association for Promoting the Discovery of Africa's Interior. The book covers the Hedjaz territories Muslims regard as sacred, with Mecca and Medina at its heart. An editor's preface links it to Burckhardt's Nubia and Syria volumes.

Those earlier travels won favor for merit and for their editor's fame as scholar and geographer. This volume, long delayed, proves no less worthy, the preface insists. It remains a classic of Arabian travel, careful, observant, and first-hand.
9588-my-summer-with-dr-singletary-part-2:
Part two of Whittier's Tales and Sketches holds My Summer with Dr. Singletary, a fragment of a tale. The piece opens on the doctor's death, then asks why this one man's life should claim our care. Singletary, an old man of odd ways, seldom left his home in later years. Yet death, Whittier writes, lifts the veil and shows the man as God's child, brother to us all.

The fragment meditates on joy and sorrow, pride and folly, and the sympathy owed to every life. Its tone is grave and tender, more essay than plot. A reader gets a short, thoughtful Whittier prose piece, and a glimpse of his Quaker faith in the worth of each soul.
9776-cicero-s-brutus-or-history-of-famou:
Cicero's Brutus, or History of Famous Orators, with his Orator, appears here in E. Jones's English translation, the first in the tongue. Jones notes that Cicero's fame needs no praise, and that the Brutus grew from his retirement during the civil war's African close. Cast as a dialogue, it sketches Greek and Roman speakers down to Cicero's own day. Lives and speeches blend into a hidden epitome of Roman history.

The Orator beside it defines the accomplished speaker, the ideal toward which the histories point. Jones writes for readers new to rhetoric. A reader gets Cicero's own school of eloquence, with lives of orators and a standard for great speech.
9811-the-adventures-of-hugh-trevor:
Thomas Holcroft's novel follows Hugh Trevor, a young man born into a family quarrel over rank and marriage. His rector grandfather disowns his mother for wedding a farmer's son, and Hugh grows up with little money and fewer prospects in late eighteenth-century England.

Told in Hugh's own voice, the story sends him through a string of jobs, patrons, and schemes as he tries to earn a living by his wits. Along the way Holcroft pokes fun at snobbery, the law, the stage, and politics. It is a lively, talkative picture of how a clever outsider climbed, stumbled, and kept going.
a-sketch-of-the-life-of-brig-gen-francis:
William Dobein James, who served as one of Marion's militia, wrote this life of Brigadier General Francis Marion and the history of his brigade. The title page dates the work to April 1821 and covers the brigade from its rise in June 1780 to its end in December 1782. An appendix prints letters between leading men of the day, chiefly from General Greene to Marion.

Four chapters move from Marion's early life through the campaigns of 1780, 1781, and 1782 in South Carolina. James describes marches, ambushes, and the men who rode with the famous partisan leader. Because the author was there, his account stays close to the ground and to daily hardship.
a-woman-s-way-through-unknown-labrador:
Mina Hubbard's A Woman's Way Through Unknown Labrador tells how she finished the journey that killed her husband. Leonidas Hubbard starved in the Labrador interior in 1903, attempting the route from North-West River to Ungava Bay. In 1905 his widow set out to complete it. With George Elson, her husband's Cree guide, she traveled six hundred miles of unmapped river. The route ran up the Naskapi and down the George River to Ungava. Her party's race with the rival Dillon Wallace expedition gives the narrative its pulse.

Inside, the book is survey and elegy at once: maps corrected, rapids run, and a grief carried to where it happened. She was the first woman of European descent to cross Labrador's interior. Readers get a classic of women's exploration literature, written plainly by a widow who navigated by her husband's unfinished map and her own considerable nerve.
an-episode-under-the-terror:
Honoré de Balzac begins on the evening of January 22, 1793, the day after the execution of Louis XVI, as snow falls on a deserted Paris street. An old lady makes her way to a pastry shop in the Faubourg Saint Martin. She is a nun in hiding, and she comes for a box that is more than it seems. Clara Bell and others translated the tale.

A stranger follows her home through the snow, and fear gives way to a strange gratitude. The man, marked by the Terror's violence, seeks one small act of peace from the sisters. Balzac builds the short tale on dread, faith, and an uneasy mercy shown between enemies.
boy-scouts-in-a-submarine-or-searching-a:
Boy Scouts in a Submarine, or Searching an Ocean Floor, by G Harvey Ralphson, sends its scout troop under the sea in the submarine Sea Lion. Ralphson, whose series also put the boys in an airship, in Mexico, and on motor cycles, opens lost on an ocean floor, with a conflict of authority aboard. The frontispiece shows the Sea Lion equal to a night long chase, which sets the book's pace at once.

Contents promise the dandy submarine, a wolf on the trail, two wolves in a pen, and a night on the ocean floor. Jimmie, the troop's irrepressible scout, goes hunting on the bottom. He demands a medal and proves foolish like a fox. Jack makes a discovery. The secret of the hold waits its turn. Ralphson's formula mixes naval technology, adult villains, and scout resourcefulness: boys on guard under the sea, solving with pluck what professionals cannot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Saint-Victor describes the royal abbey and school of Paris, founded when William of Champeaux, archdeacon of Notre-Dame, retired in 1108 to a hermitage dedicated to St. Victor. Disciples followed him, Abelard among them, and persuaded him to lecture again.

William became a canon regular with some followers, then Bishop of Châlons in 1113 at St. Bernard's request, succeeded at Saint-Victor by Gildwin, a man of piety and learning. Popes, kings, queens and noblemen richly endowed the abbey, whose canons reformed many houses, including Sainte-Geneviève in Paris, Wigmore in Wales, and St. Augustine's in Bristol. Forty abbeys of the order appear in King Louis' last will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achard-de-sai:
Achard de Saint-Victor was a canon regular, Abbot of St-Victor in Paris, and Bishop of Avranches, born about 1100 and dead in 1172. Some authorities make him English, others place him among the Norman de Pertins of Domfront. He studied at St-Victor's school, then entered its cloister. On the death of the first abbot Gilduin in 1155, he was elected to the vacant post, when the royal abbey stood near the zenith of its glory.

Two years later the chapter of Seez elected him bishop, confirmed by Adrian IV, but Henry II intruded his chaplain Roger instead. Relations with the Plantagenet later turned cordial, and Achard used his influence to make the royal treasurer pay money unjustly kept from the poor. Raised to Avranches in 1162, he stood godfather to Henry's daughter Elinor, and he wrote on the seven deserts of the soul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-st-vi:
Adam of St. Victor, a prominent, prolific Latin hymn writer, was born late in the twelfth century, probably at Paris, who died in the Abbey of St. Victor, then in Paris's suburbs, sometime between 1172 and 1192. Contemporaries styled him Brito, meaning Briton or Breton, but his Paris education and early abbey entry make him presumably French, living in the abbey, something of a theological centre, until his death.

Adam is the most illustrious exponent of the twelfth century's revival of liturgical poetry, and Archbishop Trench ranks him first among the Middle Ages' sacred Latin poets. Some thirty-seven of his hymns and sequences appeared in Clichtoveus's Elucidatorium Ecclesiasticum, and nearly seventy more, preserved at St. Victor until the Revolution, were found in the Bibliotheque Nationale by Leon Gautier, who edited the first complete edition in 1858.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-administrator:
Administrator, generally, means a person who manages common affairs for a time. He acts not in his own name, nor by an office's ordinary jurisdiction, but in a superior's name and by a superior's authority, delegated to him. In this sense vicars, prefects-apostolic, and vicars-capitular — even vicars-general — sometimes count as administrators.

In the stricter sense, modern writers apply the term to a person, usually a cleric and rarely a layman. He is given provisional administration of church affairs by special papal or episcopal appointment. Though delegated, his power may be quasi-ordinary, with a right to subdelegate, and its extent depends entirely on his commission. It may cover temporalities only, spiritual matters only, or both. Three kinds deserve special mention: administrators of dioceses, of parishes, and of ecclesiastical institutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-bic:
Alexander Bicknor was Archbishop of Dublin, of a Kent family, elected in 1310 while Prebendary of Maynooth and Treasurer of Ireland, and dead in 1349. Edward II set his election aside for Lech, who soon died, and after petitions in 1314 and 1317, Bicknor was finally consecrated at Rome on 22 July 1317. In 1318 he attended the English Parliament and helped promulgate at St. Paul's the excommunication of Robert Bruce.

Though often abroad as a diplomat, Bicknor served his diocese by building an episcopal residence and trying, without success, to attach a college to St. Patrick's Cathedral. He went on embassies to France in 1323 and 1324, negotiating peace and a Spanish match for Edward, Prince of Wales, and failed in both. On his return Edward II charged him over the loss of La Rozelle, and Bicknor joined Queen Isabella in plotting the overthrow of the Despensers, the royal favourites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexis-franco:
Alexis-François Artaud de Montor was a French diplomat and historian, born at Paris in July 1772 and dead there in November 1849. An émigré during the Revolution, he carried missions to the Holy See for the royal princes and served in Condé's army in the Champagne campaign. Bonaparte named him to the French Legation at Rome as secretary. He held the post under Cacault, left briefly when Chateaubriand arrived with Cardinal Fesch, and resumed after Chateaubriand resigned.

As chargé d'affaires to Florence in 1805, Artaud was recalled in 1807 on a false suspicion of favouring the Queen of Etruria. He served as censor late in the Empire. Under the Restoration he was embassy secretary at Vienna and again at Rome, retiring on a pension in 1830 to write. Besides a highly rated translation of Dante's Divine Comedy, he wrote histories of Pius VII, Dante, the popes, Leo XII, and Pius VIII.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloysius-schl:
Aloysius Schlor was an ascetical writer, born at Vienna in 1805 and dead at Graz in 1852. After Vienna studies he was ordained in 1828, chaplain at Altlerchenfeld. In 1831 he became Vienna seminary prefect of studies, earning his doctorate in 1832. Two years later he became Frintaneum spiritual director, court chaplain, and confessor to Emperor Ferdinand. He resigned in 1837, laboured as Verona chaplain for Germans, joined the Diocese of Seckau, and became Graz seminary spiritual director.

There he spent his remaining days working for the Austrian clergy's reformation, especially by reintroducing retreats and by his writings. Principal works: Why Am I Catholic? (1834 to 1837); Jesus My Desire, a valued prayerbook of 1835; Philanthropy of Faith, or Verona Church Life in Recent Times, 1839. Then came Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius (1840); Clericus Orans et Meditans (1841); The Spiritual Guide (1842); The Cleric in Solitude (1844); Meditations for Priests and Clerics, three volumes (1847). His sermons appeared in 1851; his Lenten sermons separately in 1905.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-protect:
The altar protector, also called vesperale, stragulum, or altar cover, is a cloth, baize, or velvet cover laid on the altar table when no sacred function is taking place. It shields the altar cloth from stains and soil. It runs slightly wider than the table and somewhat longer, hanging several inches down each side and the front. Any colour may be used, green or red preferred, its front and side edges usually scalloped, embroidered, or fringed.

It is removed during divine services, except at Vespers, when only the table's front need be uncovered for the Magnificat incensing, the cover simply turned back. It need not be blessed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiphonary-o:
An ancient Latin manuscript supposedly first written at Bangor, Ireland. Muratori found the codex in Milan's Ambrosian Library and named it the Antiphonary of Bangor. Cardinal Federigo Borromeo had brought it from Bobbio with many books when founding that library in 1609. Bobbio, in an Apennine gorge northeast of Genoa, was founded by St. Columbanus, disciple of St. Comgal, founder of Bangor's great monastery on Belfast Lough in County Down. St. Columbanus died at Bobbio and was buried there in 615. This links Bobbio and Bangor at once, and the codex's contents prove it originally a Bangor book.

Its contents, ill-suited to the name Antiphonary, run: six canticles, twelve hymns, sixty-nine hour collects, special collects, seventy anthems, the Creed, the Pater Noster. The most famous item is the original Creed of Nicaea. It lacks the Filioque clause, merely stating the three Persons' homoousia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonis-van-d:
Dutch painter Antonis Mor, commonly called Antonio Moro or Anthonis More, was born at Utrecht in 1519 and died at Antwerp between 1576 and 1578. Trained first under Jan van Scorel, his earliest work is probably a portrait at Stockholm dated 1538, with other early pictures at Utrecht, Berlin, and Lille still debated for authenticity. In 1547 he joined the Guild of St. Luke at Antwerp, and soon Cardinal Granvelle, bishop of Arras, became his steady patron and introduced him to Emperor Charles V.

Portraits of Granvelle himself and of the Duke of Alba stand out from the start of that patronage. A first visit to Italy about 1550 took him to Rome, where he copied older masters. The article follows a portraitist who rose from guild member to court painter, prized for grave, lifelike likenesses of rulers and churchmen across Europe. His career shows how a painter's fortunes could turn on one powerful patron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-exe:
An apostolic executor is a cleric who carries out a papal rescript, putting into effect what is needed for it to work. For matters touching religious orders, the executor of apostolic letters is the order's superior, its general or provincial. When favours are granted directly to petitioners, the executor simply executes the favour. He has no duty to judge the grant's wisdom, unless it is notorious that the favour was obtained by stealth.

Rescripts usually go not to the parties but, in the external forum, or public church court, to the local ordinary. In the internal forum, or conscience, they go to any approved confessor chosen by the people concerned. In that last case the grant rests wholly on the executor's judgment and conscience, with delegated power to decide. The entry maps a small but vital office: the person who turns a papal paper into action.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apparitor: An apparitor is the official name for an officer of church courts. He serves summonses, arrests an accused person, and, in church-civil procedure, takes possession of disputed property, physically or formally, to secure execution of the judge's sentence. That role applies where the church court is recognized in its full standing. He thus serves as constable and sheriff. His guarantee of delivery proves the summoned person knew the duty to appear, and his statement grounds a charge of contumacy, or stubborn refusal, against anyone who disobeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arator:
Arator, a Christian poet of the sixth century, likely of Ligurian origin, studied at Milan under Bishop Laurentius and Ennodius. Then he went to Ravenna on the advice of Parthenius, Ennodius's nephew. He became a lawyer and won Theodoric's distinction for an oration on behalf of the Dalmatians. He entered Gothic court service under Cassiodorus's protection, resigning about 536 during the struggle with Byzantium. Pope Vigilius then made him subdeacon of the Roman church.

Then he wrote in hexameters, six-foot verse lines, two books On the Acts of the Apostles. The first, dedicated to Peter, ends with chapter twelve; the second, dedicated to Paul, ends with the martyrdom of both apostles. Many events are skipped or barely touched, for Arator aimed at mystical and moral meaning, offering strange readings of numbers and names and praising Peter at Paul's expense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asia-minor:
Asia Minor is the mass Asia projects westward of a line from the Gulf of Alexandretta, or Issus, on the Mediterranean to near Trebizond, or Trapezus, on the Black Sea. Washed by the Black Sea to the north, the Mediterranean to the south, and the Aegean to the west, it spans latitudes 36 to 42 north. Its longitudes run 26 to 40 east. It is about 720 miles long at most and 420 broad, averaging 650 by 300 miles.

At its western tip it almost touches Europe, separated only by the Bosphorus and Dardanelles straits and the small Sea of Marmora, through which Mediterranean and Black Sea meet. In remote antiquity it had no common name, being known by its races or kingdoms. The long article then surveys land, peoples, and history, above all the peninsula's place in early Christianity, from Paul's journeys to Byzantine sees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auditor:
An auditor, in this church-law sense, was an official of the Roman Curia whose task was to hear and examine cases laid before the pope. The name comes from the Latin audire, to hear. Such officials could not decide a case unless the pope gave them delegated jurisdiction, so they were not judges in the strict sense. They had formed part of the Curia since the Middle Ages.

Three leading auditors are described. The Auditor Papae first advised the pope, then gained judicial power, though since 1831 his work has been limited to church affairs such as testing candidates for Italian bishoprics. The Auditor Camerae once judged appeals and even bishops, but his tribunal now mainly speeds commissions. The Auditors of the Rota, named for the round table where they sat, now give opinions on beatification cases and questions of precedence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auxentius-jun:
Auxentius Junior, born Mercurinus, was a Scythian disciple of Ulfilas, the apostle to the Goths, whose life and death he described. That account reached print when the Arian bishop Maximinus included it in 383 in a work against St Ambrose and the Synod of Aquileia of 381. Mercurinus, renamed Auxentius, became the favorite of the Empress Justina. Milan's Arians set him up as anti-bishop against Ambrose at his election.

In 386 he challenged Ambrose to a public dispute, with judges drawn from the Arian empress's court favorites, and he demanded the Basilica Portiana for Arian use. Ambrose refused to yield the church, and a siege followed, with Ambrose and a crowd of faithful Milanese shut inside the building. The empress at last abandoned her favorite and made peace with Ambrose. The entry cites Baunard's life of Ambrose and Hefele's councils for the episode.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bangor:
Bangor, anciently Bangor Vawr, is a Welsh diocese on the Menai Straits in Carnarvonshire. It must not be confused with Bangor Iscoed in Wales or the Irish monastery of Bangor in County Down. Its see is traditionally founded by St Daniel, or Deiniol, near the close of the sixth century. His death is dated 544, 554, or 584, though recent research calls even 584 too early.

Before the Norman Conquest the diocese's history is so obscure that Godwin allowed no bishops before the Normans. In 1092 Hervey, a court cleric of William Rufus, became bishop and attended Anselm's Westminster council, the first Welsh bishop at an English council. His people resented a stranger ignorant of their language, and violent measures ended in bloodshed and his flight to England. Translated to Ely in 1108, he left a cathedral that remains England and Wales's smallest and humblest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beelphegor:
Beelphegor, or Baalpeor, was the baal of Mount Phogor in Moab, baal meaning the possessor who holds real domination. Some identify him with Chemosh, Moab's national god, but local deities often stood distinct in the popular mind. Baal worship credited him with soil fertility and flock increase, honored by offerings and often by unchaste rites.

Israel met him at Settim, on Moab's plains, their last station before Canaan. There many Israelites, after intercourse with Moabite women, joined sacrificial banquets to Beelphegor and were punished by death. Numbers 25 tells the tale, and Paul cites the chastisement as a moral in 1 Corinthians. Whether immoral rites belonged to his cult is likely but not certain from the text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cantor:
A cantor, also called precentor, is the chief singer and sometimes the instructor of a church choir. The entry describes a leader who starts every chant and guides the melody by hand. He watches to prevent or correct mistakes among the singers under him. In the Gregorian Schola Cantorum the role once belonged to an officer called Prior scholae or Primicerius.

Cathedral cantors of the Middle Ages ranked among the chapter dignitaries and mastered music and chant. By the fourteenth century many handed teaching to a master of music. Harmonized music later shifted duties toward a conductor or lay choir-master. Seated at the choir's right with the succentor at his left, the cantor often carried a staff as a mark of dignity. That custom survives in some places.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capuchin-fria:
The Capuchins form a self-governing branch of the first Franciscan Order, alongside the Observants and the Conventuals. Their reform dates from 1525 and grew in the Marches, an Italian province where Franciscan simplicity held deep roots. The friars there held fast to the order's early simplicity. The entry traces the reform to a call to observe the Rule to the letter.

A long pointed hood made from the cappa gave the reform its name and habit. Papal approval followed, with ultramontane provinces allowed and full independence under an elected minister general from 1619. Missions spread by 1662 from the Congo and Morocco to Brazil and Canada, while England received its first friars in 1599 and the United States gained provinces from 1857.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal-prot:
A cardinal protector is a cardinal charged since the thirteenth century with special care in the Roman Curia for a religious order, confraternity, church, college, city, or nation. He pleaded its causes, defended it when unjustly accused, and sought the Holy See's aid when its rights, property, or interests were threatened. The office mirrors the ancient Roman patron, who stood for a client city before imperial Rome.

Cicero, patron of Dyrrachium and Capua, shows how the Roman model worked. The Claudian family, protectors of Sicily and the Peloponnesus, shows how it even became hereditary. The Church adopted the pattern for external administration, though the Lateran Council of 1512 urged cardinals to act without partiality or human respect. Today, the entry notes, Portugal alone among states keeps a cardinal protector.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-o-con:
An entry on Charles O'Conor, the Irish scholar often called the Venerable, who almost alone in his age preserved Ireland's written past. Born at Belanagare, County Roscommon, in 1710 to an ancient Catholic family, he read Irish manuscripts with a mathematical eye. He noted dates of kings, princes, and foundations in the margins and flagged contradictions. Irish was his native tongue, and he kept alive traditions that were fading around him.

O'Conor's Dissertations on the History of Ireland appeared in 1753, drew him into correspondence with Samuel Johnson, who urged him to write on pre-Norman Ireland. His manuscript collection passed to his grandson and became the famed Stowe Collection. It holds the Stowe Missal and a portion of the Four Masters' Annals, now housed in the Royal Irish Academy. With Dr. Curry he also founded the Catholic Committee in 1757, acting as a lay spokesman for Irish Catholics. He died in 1791.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerics-of-sa:
Saint Viator, lector of the Lyons cathedral in the fourth century, gives the earliest type of cathedral-school teacher. Reading and expounding Scripture to the people and catechising children, he won high esteem from his bishop, Saint Just, and the Lyons flock. After Aquileia in 381, Just retired to the solitudes of Thebais, taking Viator as companion of his exile. Both died in sanctity at a monastery of Scete in 389.

Because Viator sanctified himself teaching the young, he became patron of the Clerics of Saint Viator. Father Louis-Joseph Querbes, pastor of Vourles near Lyons, founded the community in 1835. Seeking Christian teachers after the Reign of Terror, he had opened a lay-teacher school at Vourles in 1829. In 1835 his band became a community of priests and brothers under vows, approved by Lyons. Gregory the Sixteenth approved its statutes in 1838, with help from the Roman Jesuits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confessor:
Camillo Beccari's entry traces confessor, from Latin confiteri, to confess or profess, a word unknown to classical writers and first used by Christians. It honored champions who confessed Christ openly under persecution and suffered prison, torture, exile, or mine labor, staying faithful to life's end. Martyrs differed: they died for the faith. An epitaph recorded by De Rossi marks the distinction early, naming Aurelius Diogenes confessor beside Valeria Felicissima and others.

After the mid-fourth century the title widened to men of virtue and knowledge who confessed Christ before the world by preaching and holy life. Modern use ties it to canonization practice, since popes reserved sainthood decisions: confessor pontiff, non-pontiff, or doctor, approved by miracles and solemnly judged for veneration. The entry points readers to martyrs, persecutions, and beatification for the wider frame, and to the Sacrament of Penance for the priest as confessor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confiteor:
Adrian Fortescue's entry treats the Confiteor, named from its first word, I confess. It is a general confession of sins, used in the Roman Rite at Mass's start and on other occasions as grace preparation. History opens with sacramental confession and Mass. Both original Eastern liturgies begin with the celebrant's confession of sin. Early Roman sacramentaries and ordos say nothing of it, picturing Mass starting at the Introit. In some form it likely served early as a private sacristy prayer before Mass.

Use varies. Sometimes it runs double, mutual confession by celebrant to people, then by people to him. Sometimes it runs single. As a single form it appears in Mass's opening prayers after Psalm Judica me, again when others communicate, and when Communion is given outside Mass. Its words, Fortescue says, are too well known to quote. Sources run from Missal and Ritual to Bona, Benedict XIV, and Gihr.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conservator:
William Fanning's entry defines a conservator, from Latin conservare, as a papal judge defending favored persons, universities, orders, and the poor from open injury without process. Conservators appear as early as the thirteenth century. Innocent IV assumes them in a decree first revealing their power. Abuses moved Trent to limit them, yet controversies led Clement VIII, Gregory XV, and Innocent X to define their rights precisely.

Troubles moved Clement XIII on 23 April 1762 to end such officials in missionary countries, referring controversies to the Holy See. From then conservators fell into desuetude. Law required choice from cathedral leaders, later from synodal judges. Regulars' chosen conservator held five years secure without cause. He lacked power where examination was required, heard all complaints against regulars, yet heard regulars' complaints against others only when open, deciding swiftly. He could punish even high leaders blocking him, but power stayed within his one diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-curator:
A canon law entry defines the curator as a person legally appointed to administer another's property when age or incapacity prevents self-management. Curators are often confused with tutors, but they differ sharply. Tutors guard persons first and property second, and serve minors only. Curators serve mainly temporal concerns, for persons of any age, and may be appointed for one determined duty.

Curators are constituted for the mentally weak, prodigals, and habitual gamblers, though luxurious living alone never justifies removing control of property. They may also serve captives, the absent, and the deaf and dumb, but a husband may not act as curator for his wife. Before administering, a curator must give bond for fidelity, and a judge fixes any salary. Negligent loss obliges restitution in conscience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doctor:
Doctor, from the Latin for to teach, is the title of an authorized teacher. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry finds doctors beside princes and elders in Deuteronomy, and hears Azarias foretell days without priest, teacher, or law. Their duty was to expound the law, and Christ himself was found in the Temple among the doctors. Later Jewish teachers bore titles drawn from the Talmud.

Under the New Law, doctors are those gifted to teach the faith, and the entry moves from Scripture to the medieval universities. It traces how the teaching office grew into the academic doctorate of Paris, Oxford, and the German schools. For readers, it links a Bible word to the degree still prized in the schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-down-and-conn:
Down and Connor are two Irish dioceses whose boundary runs from Whitehouse on Belfast Lough west to the Clady River and on to Lough Neagh. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry maps the line with care. North of it, to the sea and the Bann, lies Connor, covering most of Antrim and a scrap of Derry. South of it lies Down, with the rest of Antrim and all of County Down save two baronies.

Together the sees span nearly six hundred thousand Irish acres. Each gathers ancient sees founded in Saint Patrick's time, Raholp among them in Down. The entry draws on Brady, Lanigan, Healy, and the Irish directories to trace bishops and parishes across a land where old foundations still shape the modern map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecuador:
Ecuador is an independent state of South America, bounded by Colombia in the north, Brazil in the east, Peru in the south, and the Pacific in the west. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that the equator crosses its northwest corner, giving the country its name. No part of America has drawn so much large-scale scientific exploration, above all geographic and physiographic, in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

One French expedition of 1735 measured the meridian near the equator, recalling La Condamine and Bouguer. Another, from 1790 to 1804, forever links Alexander von Humboldt to the New World. Ecuador ranks third smallest among South American republics, and the entry closes with travels, church histories, and Medina's history of printing at Quito.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-error:
Error, reduplicatively regarded, is in one way or another the product of ignorance. But besides the lack of information it implies, it adds a positive mental judgment, by which something false is held to be true, or something true avouched to be false.

In the first case, one goes wrong about whether a law exists, or whether a case falls under it. In the second, one goes wrong about a fact or some aspect of a fact. Thus, a Catholic who convinces himself there is no Friday abstinence law errs about the law. If, knowing the Church's precept, he wrongly thinks a particular Friday is not Friday, he errs about the fact.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fiscal-procur:
The fiscal procurator is the church law officer who prevents crime and safeguards ecclesiastical law. Like a state attorney in criminal cases, he brings proceedings and represents the law. The office grew from the king's procurators of thirteenth-century France. Canon law once allowed private accusation, but now all criminal cases start with the procurator.

In 1880 the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars stressed his need in every episcopal curia. Kindred officers defend marriage ties, sacred orders, and vows against attack. In canonization causes the promotor fidei argues every objection, earning the name devil's advocate. The Holy Office keeps its own fiscal officer for heresy and kindred crimes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frances-marga:
Frances Margaret Taylor, known in religion as Mother Mary Magdalen Taylor, was born on 20 January 1832 and died in London on 9 June 1900. She founded and led the Poor Servants of the Mother of God. Her father was a Protestant clergyman, and her youth was spent in charity among the poor of his Lincolnshire parish. In 1854 patriotism took her to the Crimean War as a nurse on Florence Nightingale's staff. Contact with Catholic priests, Sisters of Mercy, and soldiers opened her eyes to the Catholic faith.

Received into the Church after instruction, she worked among London's poor, and with Lady Georgiana Fullerton laid the foundations of her institute, opening refuges, convents, and schools. She also wrote stories for the faith and edited The Lamp. She helped start The Month and The Messenger of the Sacred Heart, spreading devotion to the Sacred Heart with tireless energy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gloria-laus-e:
Gloria, laus et honor is a hymn composed by Saint Theodulph of Orléans in 810, in Latin elegiacs. The Roman Missal takes its first six couplets for the hymn after the Palm Sunday procession, the use to which it was always dedicated. A Catholic Encyclopedia article describes the antiphonal singing that opens the church door.

Chanters inside the closed door sing the first couplet, Glory, praise, and honor to you, King Christ, Redeemer, and the processional chorus outside repeats it. Each following couplet is answered the same way. The subdeacon strikes the door with the staff of the cross, the door opens, and the procession enters. Founded on Psalm 23, Psalm 117, Matthew 21, and Luke 19, the hymn was assigned in the Middle Ages to boy chanters at Salisbury, York, Hereford, and Rouen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-the-i:
Gregory the Illuminator, born about 257 and dead about 337, stands in this reference entry as Armenia's apostle, national saint, and patron. The entry places him against an older Christian presence in Armenia. It then follows his part in the kingdom's turn to the new faith under King Trdat, also called Tiridates, while Diocletian ruled as emperor.

Raised as a Christian at Caesarea in Cappadocia, Gregory was ordained bishop of the Armenians there. He set up bishops across the land from Ashtishat, preaching and holding worship in the Armenian tongue. Temples became churches and crowds were baptized. The entry also weighs the famous life by Agathangelos, with its pit, tortures. The king turned into a boar, against what can be known with more certainty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gyor:
Hungary's Diocese of Győr, suffragan of Gran, took its present shape in 1777, when Vas and parts of Veszprém went to form Szombathely. What remained was Moson, Sopron, most of Győr county, and part of Komárom. Founded by King St. Stephen about 1001, it holds 239 parishes, 379 clergy, two seminaries with 102 students, and 48 monasteries with 630 religious among 451,150 Catholics.

Its bishops include Hartvik, who wrote St. Stephen's life, Thomas Bakócz, later primate and cardinal, and Georg Draskovich, a champion of the Counter-Reformation, while another Draskovich fled the Turks with his chapter. Martinus Pethe restored the cathedral after the reconquest, Demetrius Náprágyi brought St. Ladislaus's skull reliquary from Grosswardein in 1608. Johann Simor stands as its most illustrious recent bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-habor:
Mesopotamia's Habor river, still called the Habur, runs about two hundred miles from Mount Masius through desert country to join the Euphrates at Carchemish, watering fertile banks on its winding course. Its chief tributary, the Jeruyer or ancient Mygdonius, passes Nisibis before joining it. The district of Gozan along its banks gave it the Bible's name, river of Gozan.

Cuneiform inscriptions name the Habor under Tiglath-pileser I and Asshurnasir-pal. The books of Kings and Chronicles place Israel's exiles there under Tiglath-pileser III and Salmanasar IV. The entry warns against confusing this river with Ezekiel's Chobar canal east of the Tigris, and notes Benjamin of Tudela finding some two hundred Jews near its mouth in 1163.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-st-vi:
Hugh of St. Victor was a medieval philosopher, theologian, and mystical writer, born in 1096 at Hartingham in Saxony and dead in 1141. Eldest son of Conrad, count of Blankenburg, he was schooled at St. Pancras near Halberstadt, where his uncle Reinhard, bishop of Halberstadt, had studied under William of Champeaux. Against his parents' opposition, Hugh joined the Canons Regular of St. Augustine there.

Before finishing his novitiate, disturbed times led his uncle to send him to St. Victor in Paris, where he arrived about 1115. Under Gilduin, successor to founder William of Champeaux, Hugh spent his life studying, teaching, and writing. On Thomas's death in 1133 he became head of the School of St. Victor, which under him reached brilliant success, and his works shaped medieval theology and mysticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-mayor:
John Mayor, also called Major or Mair, was a Scottish scholastic philosopher and historian who taught John Knox. Born near Haddington in 1496, he studied at Oxford, Cambridge, and Paris, graduating master of arts in 1494 and doctor of theology in 1505. He taught logic and theology at Paris, Glasgow, and Saint Andrews, ending as provost of Saint Salvator's College from 1530 until his death in 1550.

One of the greatest scholastics of his time, he counted Knox, Patrick Hamilton, and George Buchanan among his pupils. In philosophy he led the nominalist tendency at Paris. As a canonist he placed chief church authority in the whole Church rather than the pope. In politics he held that civil authority comes from the people, who may reclaim it by force if needed. His History of Greater Britain of 1521, in barbarous Latin, faithfully shows his vigor and independence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jorge-de-mont:
Jorge de Montemayor was a Portuguese-born writer who holds a prominent place in Spanish letters for his pastoral novel La Diana. Born at Montemor about 1520, he was no university man, not even acquainted with Latin, and little is known of his life beyond his work.

La Diana, published at Valencia by common report in 1542 but judged from its allusions to date after 1554, probably 1558 or 1559, long served as the model for pastoral novels. Written in good Spanish, it tells incidents from the author's own life, including an unfortunate love affair, with prose better than its verse, and a promised sequel that never appeared. Three continuations followed, and the book inspired Lope de Vega's Arcadia, Cervantes's Galatea, and, it is said, Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-azor:
Juan Azor was a Spanish Jesuit moral theologian whose great work shaped conscience cases for centuries. Born at Lorca in Murcia in 1535, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1559 and taught philosophy and theology at Piacenza, Alcalá, and Rome. He served on the first committee that drew up the Jesuits' famous Ratio Studiorum, their plan of studies.

Azor's Institutiones Morales, in three folio volumes from 1600 to 1611, treats every question touching a right or wrong conscience. Praised by Pope Clement VIII and reprinted at Brescia, Venice, Lyons, Cologne, and Paris, it stayed in high regard with St. Alphonsus Liguori. He died at Rome in 1603.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lector:
A lector, or reader, in the West holds the second of the four minor orders, and Eastern Churches likewise ordain readers to a minor order before the diaconate. The office arose from sheer need for educated persons able to read books aloud in church, continuing the Jewish practice of public Scripture reading.

Justin Martyr about 165 first mentions a Christian liturgical reader, and the homily called Second Clement also names one. The post was honourable and demanded schooling above most offices, and readers often went on to expound what they read, though Justin assigns preaching to the bishop. Readers were blessed and set apart by prayer and ceremony, like grave-diggers, registrars, and widows. In early centuries lectors read all lessons, Epistle and Gospel included, and Rome under Cornelius counted readers among its fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-little-sister:
The Little Sisters of the Poor are a congregation that shelters and cares for helpless old people, founded at St. Servan in Brittany in 1839. Young working women began by looking after one poor blind woman, then took in more aged folk, living on daily earnings and alms.

A later editor's note in the hosted text corrects the 1913 account. It says Jeanne Jugan, not Abbe Le Pailleur, was the true foundress, and that she was beatified in 1982. Sisters take simple lasting vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, plus a fourth vow of hospitality, and their rule rests on St. Augustine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marius-mercat:
Marius Mercator was a church writer, probably born in North Africa about 390 and dead shortly after 451. In 417 or 418 he was at Rome, writing two anti-Pelagian treatises for St Augustine. From 429 to about 448 he lived at Constantinople. His works, mostly translations and excerpts from Greek writers, heretical and orthodox alike, were edited by Garnier in 1673 and reprinted by Migne.

Against Pelagians he wrote two Commonitoria, one on Caelestius's name and one against the Pelagian heresy and Julian's writings. The first helped drive Julian of Eclanum and Caelestius from Constantinople and win their censure at Ephesus in 431. Against Nestorians he wrote a letter setting Nestorius's errors apart from the views of Paul of Samosata, Ebion, Photinus, and Marcellus, plus twelve chapters of Nestorius's blasphemies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-tudor:
Mary Tudor was Queen of England from 1553 to 1558, born 18 February 1516 and dead 17 November 1558. Daughter and only surviving child of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, she had Cardinal Wolsey as godfather and counted Cardinal Pole and his mother, the Countess of Salisbury, among early intimates. Modest, affectionate, and kindly by nature, she spoke Latin, French, and Spanish with ease and played music accomplishedly.

When Henry died, Mary retired into obscurity under young Edward's influences, but at his death on 6 July 1553 Northumberland hid the news and schemed for Lady Jane Grey. Mary's success proved highly popular, and late-administration friends hastened to make peace. Her severity in later years, clashing with lifelong clemency and generosity, may owe something to bitterness concentrated in those years, as chronic dropsy made her a doomed woman.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mediator-chri:
Christ as Mediator treats the one who brings estranged parties to friendly agreement. In New Testament theology the estranged parties are always God and man, and the title belongs to Christ alone. When angels, saints, or holy men plead our cause before God, they mediate with Christ; their work is secondary and better called intercession. Moses stands as the proper mediator of the Old Testament.

Paul writes to Timothy that God our Saviour wills all men to be saved and to know the truth. For there is one God and one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as ransom for all. His fitness lies in his manhood, his performance in his redeeming sacrifice and witness to truth, and his aim in mankind's salvation and knowledge of God. The entry then weighs his qualifications, his performance, and his results, placing his mediation at the heart of salvation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minor:
Minor, from the Latin minor, means that which is less or inferior in comparison with another, and the term is used of things as well as persons. Among things, we may mention causae minores, matters of lesser importance, as opposed to causae majores, the more important. Minor benefices stand opposed to major benefices, which imply jurisdiction and are confirmed in papal consistory. Minor churches are those of inferior rank.

The minor excommunication, now out of use, stood opposed to the major excommunication. In reference to persons, certain uses of minor depend on usage rather than definition: minors in age, minors in religious orders, and the Friars Minor, whose very name claims littleness. The article sorts these varied applications with canon law precision.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monsignor:
Monsignor, from Latin for my lord, has served since the fourteenth century as a title for persons high in rank or power. This entry follows its shifting fortunes in court and church. French nobles once demanded it from dependents. In royal usage it marked the Dauphin or heir presumptive. Monsieur belonged to the king's eldest brother.

In church life the title now signals a distinction granted by the highest ecclesiastical authority. Its grades include domestic prelates and chamberlains, each with its dress and privileges. Bourbon claimants still assume it by courtesy. The entry sorts the civil title's decline, the ecclesiastical grades, and the rules for addressing and styling each rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-thabor:
Mount Thabor, called Itabyrion by the ancients and Jebel et Tur by the Arabs, stands out among Palestine's mountains. Its picturesque site, graceful outline, rich vegetation on calcareous rock, and splendid summit views set it apart. Nearly isolated and almost hemispherical, it rises 1,650 feet above the Plain of Esdraelon about five miles southeast of Nazareth.

Its summit forms an oblong plateau 3,000 feet long, commanding Hermon to the northeast, the Jordan Valley, the Lake of Tiberias and the ranges of Hauran, Bashan and Gilead. Tradition makes Thabor the mount of the Transfiguration, and the entry weighs that claim against Hermon. It traces its fortress history from Josephus through the Crusades, and describes the churches that crown it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nabuchodonoso:
Nabuchodonosor is the form nearest the Babylonian Nabu-kudurri-usur, nearer than Nebuchadrezzar and especially Nebuchadnezzar from the Massoretic transliteration. Its second part is variously read as a prayer to Nebo to defend crown, tiara, empire, landmark or work. Two kings of the name ruled Babylon.

Nabuchodonosor I, about 1152 to 1124, was the most famous monarch of the Pashi or Isin dynasty. A prince of untiring energy, he led Chaldean armies to victory east and west against Lulubi, Elam and Syria. Twice beaten by the Assyrian king Ashshur-resh-ishi, he still checked for a time the decay of the first Babylonian Empire. Nabuchodonosor II, about 605 to 562, son of Nabopolassar, reigned forty-three years and fills many pages of Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-fria:
The Order of Friars Minor, or Franciscans, began when Francis of Assisi gathered twelve disciples and won Innocent III's verbal approval on 16 April 1209. From that small band the order spread across Europe within a generation, preaching poverty, penance, and the Gospel in towns and villages.

Its history splits at 1517 into Observants, Conventuals, and Capuchins, with reform branches like Discalced and Recollects beside them. The entry surveys legislation, habit, preaching, missions, learning, and saints, with statistics from 1260 to 1909 and a survey of Britain, Ireland, and America. Francis appeared before Innocent III, who gave verbal sanction to the rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pastor:
A pastor is a priest holding the cure of souls, bound by office to foster the faithful's spiritual welfare through preaching, sacraments, and paternal governance. His powers include supervision, precepts, and light corrections, but differ from a bishop's legislative, judicial, and coercive powers. A pastor counts strictly as a parish priest, or parochus, when he holds the cure in his own name over a set flock bound to seek certain sacraments from him.

Pastors, parish priests or not, are irremovable or movable. An irremovable pastor holds tenure for life, removable only for a canonical reason, and after trial on a criminal charge. A movable pastor lacks that right, yet the bishop needs a just and proportionate reason to dismiss or transfer him against his will. A wronged priest may appeal to the Holy See, and later pages treat appointment, residence, and support.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-cantor:
Peter Cantor was a twelfth-century Paris theologian whose surname came from his office. Born probably near Beauvais, he studied at Reims and taught theology for years at Paris, where he held the cantor's post from about 1180. His name appears on many charters, and popes often picked him as a judge, at Troyes in 1188 and at Compiègne in the royal divorce case of Ingeborg.

Honours pursued him and mostly slipped away. Tournai chose him bishop in 1191, but Reims annulled the election, and he is said to have refused Paris itself in 1196. That year he became dean of Reims chapter. Travelling from Paris to Reims, he fell ill at Long Pont Abbey, died there on 22 September 1197, and was buried, probably in Cistercian habit. His commentaries cover nearly all the Old Testament, best on the Psalms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-comesto:
Peter Comestor was a twelfth-century theological writer whose nickname means book-devourer. Born at Troyes, he served Notre-Dame there, became its dean before 1148, and moved about 1160 to Notre-Dame in Paris, where he replaced Odo as chancellor and ran the theological school. Alexander III let him charge a small fee for teaching licences, a favour strictly personal.

At Paris he finished the Historia Scholastica, a sacred history written for students at their own request, starting from creation and dedicated to the Bishop of Sens. Cardinal Peter of St. Chrysogonus ranked him among the three most cultured men of France. Late in life he retired to St. Victor, professed canonical life there, and was buried among its canons. His Gospel commentaries and allegories remain unpublished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-precentor:
Precentor, from Latin prae, before, and cantor, singer, marks at times a church dignitary, at times an officer of rite or rule. In old days he was the first chanter: on Sundays and great feasts he struck up antiphons, psalms, hymns, and responsories. He set the pitch for bishop and dean at Mass, while the succentor did the like for canons and clerks. He raised and taught the choir, ran its rehearsals, and watched its official work.

He bore many names, among them capiscol and primicerius. In the Middle Ages the chief dignitaries of cathedral and collegiate chapters and monastic orders took St Gregory the Great as model in leading chant schools.
