The school ever stood by when the bishop served in his cathedral, and the precentor held a place near the bishop, high in dignity. The post plainly called for deep learning and executive power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prince-henry-:
Henry the Navigator was born on 4 March 1394 and died on 13 November 1460, the fourth son of John I of Portugal and Queen Philippa, daughter of John of Gaunt. In 1415 he led the expedition that took Ceuta, Portugal's first overseas conquest, and there won his knightly spurs.  He bore blame for the disastrous Tangier attack of 1437, which cost his brother Fernando captivity and death. 

On Duarte's death, Henry backed his brother Pedro's regency claim against Queen Leonor. Later, when Pedro's soaring ambition clashed with King Affonso V, Henry could not save him from defeat and death at Alfarrobeira. Yet Henry's fame rests not on war or politics, but on opening steady seaborne exploration. As Grand Master of the Military Order of Christ, his ships warred steadily on the infidels, and in one voyage of 1418 Zarco chanced on the Madeira Islands. Henry had launched his exploring career right after Ceuta's fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prior:
A prior is a monastic superior. In St Benedict's Rule the word prior occurs often, but marks no set superior: it fits any superior, be he abbot, provost, dean, or other.  With the Cluniac reform it gained a set meaning, displacing the provost of Benedict's Rule. Hirschau's congregation, born in Germany in the eleventh century, also swapped prior for provost, and the two examples spread by degrees to all Benedictine houses and their offshoots.

Benedictines and their branches, Premonstratensians, and military orders all mark two kinds of priors. The claustral prior ranks first below the abbot, or below the grand master in military orders. He aids the abbot in ruling the house. He holds no ordinary jurisdiction by his office, since he acts wholly at the abbot's will and under his lead. His jurisdiction is thus delegated, reaching just as far as the abbot allows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-procurator:
A procurator manages another's affairs by a charge from him.  A procurator may act in court affairs, ad lites, or in affairs needing no court, ad negotia. Special procurators include the syndicus, agent of a university or corporation, and the fiscal procurator, guardian of the law in criminal proceedings.

All men, unless the law plainly bars them, may name a procurator in affairs they freely manage. The choice must shun those debarred by law. Excommunicates, notorious criminals, regulars lacking their superiors' assent, and clerics in cases where they cannot act as lawyers are barred. For court cases, those under twenty-five are barred, or for other cases, those under seventeen. A procurator must act by the charge's terms, but a general mandate covers not cases needing a special commission. He may name a substitute, save in marriages and where the affair's gravity implies he was picked with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rector:
Rector, from the Latin regere, to rule, names several offices. Mission and quasi-parish priests carry the title rector. In England and the United States some hold it permanently, as missionary rectors, while others can be removed. The title also belongs to the heads of universities, seminaries and colleges, and to the local superiors of men's religious houses.

The pope counts as rector of the world in the conferring of the tiara. At some universities, Louvain for example, the actual president bears the title rector magnificus. Rector general names the superior general of certain orders, such as the Clerics Regular of the Mother of God. In ancient times bishops ruling cities and provinces, above all in the Papal States, were called rectors, as were administrators of church lands, like the rector of Sicily. Gregory the Great uses rector as equivalent to pastor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rerum-deus-te:
Rerum Deus Tenax Vigor is the daily hymn for None in the Roman Breviary. Like the hymns for Terce and Sext, it holds only two stanzas of iambic dimeters, with a doxology that varies by feast or season. As in the hymns for Prime, Sext, and Compline, its theme is the sun's steady march marking the hours of the day. God, whose power unmoved controls nature's vastness, marks the day-hours by steady marches of the sun.

The second stanza turns that image to moral use, praying that in life's eventide God's light may abide with us, never failing. The authorship of the Terce, Sext, and None hymns is now given to Saint Ambrose only very doubtfully. The entry sets out the manuscript discussion behind that verdict, with Blume, Dreves, and Daniel among its guides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-of-st:
Richard of St Victor was a twelfth-century Scottish theologian who spent his life inside the Paris monastery of St Victor. The date and place of his birth are unknown. He was professed under the first abbot, Gilduin, and became a disciple of the mystic Hugh of St Victor, whose methods he took up and developed. He rose to sub-prior in 1159 and later to prior.

His career stayed strictly monastic, with few ties to the outside world. Yet his writings travelled widely, and other houses eagerly sought copies. Unlike Hugh, he took no interest in philosophy or in the sharp debates of his day. He distrusted secular learning as an end in itself, valuing it only when joined to knowledge of divine things. His reputation rests on mystical theology, on contemplation as the path to God, and on the orderly teaching methods he borrowed from Abelard. He died in 1173.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-salvador:
San Salvador is the name Columbus gave his first landfall in the New World, one of the Bahamas east of southern Florida at 24 degrees north and 75 degrees west. Native people called it Guanahani, and scholars have argued ever since over which island Columbus actually reached. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia weighs the rival claims without pretending to settle them.

Cat Island, Samana, Mariguana, Grand Turk, and Watling's Island have each had champions. San Salvador was the name given to Cat Island in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, yet Cat Island lacks the low, level shape and inner lagoon Columbus described. Captain Gustavus Fox argued for Samana in the Coast Survey report of 1880, and Navarrete first urged Grand Turk, leaving the puzzle open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-vigor:
Simon Vigor, French bishop and controversialist born at Evreux in Normandy about 1515, died at Carcassonne on 1 November 1575. Son of Raynaud Vigor, a court physician, he went to Paris about 1520 and studied Greek, Hebrew, Latin, then theology. Admitted to the College of Navarre in 1540, he became rector of the University of Paris that same year. In 1545 he took a doctorate in theology and became penitentiary of Evreux.

Thenceforth he preached pastorally and controversially with great success at Rouen, Paris, Metz, and elsewhere. At Saint-Germain in 1562 he defended the Catholic cause against Calvinists led by Theodore Beza. In 1563 he joined twelve Sorbonne theologians at Trent, debating clandestine marriages and indulgences with vast erudition. He also smoothed relations between Cardinal Hosius and Francisco Torres, and won Cardinal de Lorraine's confidence on a mission to Ferdinand I at Innsbruck.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th:
Founded at Rome on 8 December 1881 by Johann Baptist Jordan, as Father Francis Mary of the Cross, the Society of the Divine Savior first bore the name Society of Catholic Instruction. Jordan added a fourth vow of apostolic mission work to poverty, chastity, and obedience. Its rules draw largely on the Society of Jesus, and its black habit bears a black cincture with four knots recalling the four vows.

The Prefecture Apostolic of Assam came under the society in 1889, with 7 principal and 32 dependent stations served by 13 missionaries. A German college rose at Lochau in 1893, a station at Corvallis, Oregon, the same year, and work in Brazil began in 1896. By 1908 missions ran in thirteen languages, and the congregation counted 400 members in 35 foundations across Europe, the United States, Brazil, and Colombia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-edward-the:
Edward the Confessor, king of England from 1042 to 1066, earned his title by a reign of unusual gentleness after a youth of exile. Born in 1003 to Ethelred II and Emma of Normandy, he was sent to Normandy at ten when Danish power mastered England. Called to the throne at about forty, he was welcomed even by Danish settlers for his saintly character. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death to 5 January 1066.

His reign stayed almost unbrokenly peaceful, with the Danegelt tax remitted and no wars beyond a Welsh inroad and aid to Malcolm III against Macbeth. He married Editha, Godwin's daughter, on terms of chastity, and rebuilt Westminster Abbey in place of a promised pilgrimage. Canonized in 1161, he left laws later generations demanded back whenever they felt oppressed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teresa-lalor:
Teresa Lalor co-founded the Visitation Order in the United States with Bishop Neale of Baltimore. Born in Ireland, she died on 9 September 1846. Her Kilkenny childhood showed so clear a vocation that Bishop Lanigan arranged her entrance into his diocese's convent. Instead she had to accompany her family to America. Arriving at Philadelphia in 1797, she met Father Leonard Neale of St Joseph's, and under him gave herself to piety and charity.

Neale saw in her an instrument for a community, and an academy for girls opened. Yellow fever carried off her companions, and when Neale moved to Georgetown College in 1799, she followed to live with exiled French Poor Clares. After they left America, Lalor and two companions opened their own school within the present Visitation grounds. Pius VII granted them Visitation standing in 1816, and Mother Teresa was professed that Holy Innocents' feast, becoming first superioress of Georgetown Convent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodorus-lec:
Constantinople lector Theodorus, compiler of church history from excerpts, is the sixth-century scholar described here. Attached to Saint Sophia's church, he compiled at a friend's request the four-book Historia Tripartita, an epitome of Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret made from excerpts. An imperfect manuscript copy survives unpublished, though Valesius used it, perhaps overvaluing its readings, in editing those historians.

A two-book history carried the narrative from Theodosius II's death to Justin I's times, now lost except two long excerpt series under the spurious title Apo phones Nikephorou Kallistou. John of Damascus and the Seventh General Council's Acts quote it. Its value lies in scanty sources for an obscure age, preserved through later excerptors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-unjust-aggres: An unjust aggressor, in the moral teaching set out here, is an attacker whose violence may lawfully be met with violence. Defence of life or limb, of property of some importance, and of chastity all allow force in return, even to the point of killing the assailant. The limit is strict: only the force truly needed to stop the attack may be used, so maiming must serve instead of killing wherever maiming suffices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-hugh-tayl:
Hugh Taylor was an English martyr born at Durham, hanged, drawn, and quartered at York on 25 November 1585, not the 26th as sometimes given. He reached Reims on 2 May 1582, was ordained priest there, and was sent out on the mission on 27 March 1585. He became the first to suffer under the newly passed statute 27 Elizabeth, chapter 2, against priests.

On 26 November Marmaduke Bowes, a married gentleman, was hanged for harbouring Taylor. Challoner places Bowes at Angram Grange near Appleton in Cleveland, though he appears neither in the will of Christopher Bowes of Angram Grange, proved in 1568, nor in the 1612 pedigree. The sole evidence against Bowes came from a former tutor of his children, an apostate Catholic. The entry weighs that thin evidence with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-roger-cad:
Roger Cadwallador was an English martyr born at Stretton Sugwas near Hereford in 1568, executed at Leominster on 27 August 1610. Ordained subdeacon at Reims on 21 September 1591 and deacon the following February, he was sent in August 1592 to the English College at Valladolid, where he was ordained priest. Back in England from 1594, he worked in Herefordshire to good effect, above all among the poor, for some sixteen years.

Men searched for him in June 1605, but only at Easter 1610 was he arrested, at the house of Mrs Winefride Scroope, widow, within eight miles of Hereford. Brought before Bishop Robert Bennet, he was committed to Hereford jail, where he was loaded with irons night and day. Transferred to Leominster jail, he had to walk the whole way in shackles, though a boy was allowed to carry his cloak, before his trial and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-pa:
Thomas Palasor, or Palliser, was a Yorkshire priest executed at Durham in 1600. He reached Reims in 1592, moved on to Valladolid, and was ordained there in 1596. Returning to England, he was arrested in the house of John Norton near Lamesley in County Durham, together with Norton, his wife, and John Talbot.

All four were tried at Durham. Palasor was condemned for being a priest, and the others for assisting him. A fifth man saved himself by conforming, and Mrs Norton, believed to be pregnant, was reprieved. Palasor and his companions suffered together. The entry adds a curious sequel: an attempt by the gaoler's wife to poison the prisoners led to the conversion of her maidservant, Mary Day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-of-st-:
Walter of St Victor was a twelfth-century mystic philosopher and theologian known almost solely as prior of St Victor's monastery about 1175. Author about the Third Lateran Council of 1179 of the celebrated polemic Against the Four Labyrinths of France, and dead about 1180.

Its four labyrinths are Abelard, Gilbert de la Porrée, Peter Lombard, and Peter of Poitiers. The work bitterly attacks the dialectical method in theology, condemning in no measured terms the use of logic to elucidate the mysteries of faith. Walter raged at treating Trinity and Incarnation with scholastic levity, discarding St Victor's best traditions to abuse philosophers, theologians, and even grammarians, crying thy grammar be with thee until perdition. That violence defeated its purpose, failing to convince contemporaries and very probably hastening the triumph of the method he attacked.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-molit:
Wilhelm Molitor was a Palatinate priest who worked as poet, novelist, church lawyer, and Catholic press organizer. Born at Zweibruecken in 1819, he died at Speyer in 1880. He first trained in law at Munich and Heidelberg and held state legal posts, then turned to theology at Bonn and took orders in 1851. He became secretary to the Bishop of Speyer, a cathedral canon, and a teacher of archaeology and preaching.

Molitor led the Catholic revival in the Palatinate by founding a press association, a daily paper, and a Catholic printing house. His firm ultramontane views, backing Rome over the state, blocked his rise to the Speyer bishopric. His output was vast: poems, plays such as Kynast and Maria Magdalena, novels, sermons, church-law studies, and essays on the press, Goethe, and the stage. Rome called him to help prepare the Vatican Council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-the-c:
William the Conqueror was Duke of Normandy and King of England, the bastard son who seized a crown. Born to Robert, Duke of Normandy, and Herleva, a tanner's daughter of Falaise, he was presented to Norman nobles at seven in 1035 before Robert left on the pilgrimage that killed him. Three guardians were murdered and kidnappers threatened the boy, yet after anarchy he ruled Normandy, a youth of clean life, deep piety, and iron resolve.

In 1047 William crushed a noble rising at Val-ès-Dunes with French royal aid, took Alençon and Domfront, and mastered Maine, becoming France's mightiest vassal. A 1051 English visit, a disputed promise of the succession, and Harold's forced oath of 1064 set up his claim. When Harold broke that oath at Edward's death, William, blessed by Pope Alexander II with a consecrated banner, crossed as God's champion against perjury and won England at Hastings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-windsor:
Windsor is the Thames town in Berkshire whose castle has housed English kings for centuries. Of great antiquity, its name comes from the Saxon Windels-or, winding shore, quaintly Latinized as Ventus Morbidus in medieval papers. Saint Edward the Confessor gave the manor to Westminster Abbey, and the town became a free borough under Edward I. A palace and stronghold stood here even in Saxon Heptarchy days.

The castle's fame rests on its Round Tower mound from Saxon times, Henry III's additions, and centuries as the favourite royal home, birthplace of Edward III and Henry VI among others. Edward IV built the sumptuous Saint George's Chapel, finest perpendicular work in England, and lies buried there with successors. Under George IV nearly a million pounds rebuilt the castle to Wyatville's plans, and the chapel remains home of the Knights of the Garter.

civil-government-for-common-schools-prep:
Henry C. Northam's Civil Government for Common Schools teaches New York children their own government. Northam, a conductor of teachers' institutes at Lowville, prefaces the third edition in April 1878. Textbooks in general use, he complains, stop with theory. Students learn republican principles but not what causes a justice of the peace may try.

His manual begins with the school district and climbs to the President. Names, elections, duties, and salaries of officers fill its question-and-answer lessons. Road, school, and election districts are defined as the smallest units. The constitutions of New York, as amended in 1880, and of the United States are appended, with the Declaration of Independence. Northam wrote the art of government as practised in his state. Progressive schools, he hoped, would find the little book indispensable.

every-man-in-his-humor:
Ben Jonson's Every Man in His Humour, in the anglicized edition, carries an introduction calling Jonson the greatest English dramatist except Shakespeare. The introduction traces his Westminster schooling under Camden, to whom the play was dedicated. Jonson's soldiering in Flanders and his duels precede the comedy. The play itself reset the Italian original in London.

Old Knowell worries over his son Edward's wild companions, and sends his servant Brainworm spying after him. Master Kitely's jealousy of his wife, the water-bearer Cob, and the braggart Bobadill fill the city scenes. Every character serves his humour, the ruling obsession Jonson made a dramatic system. The comedy of humours founded a school that English drama followed for decades. Jonson's London is exact: shops, taverns, and tobacco talk. The introduction's scholarship and the play's energy make this the standard gateway to his work.
fonvizin-der-landjunker-the-minor:
A spoiled young nobleman who cannot learn and will not grow up anchors Denis Fonvizin's comedy The Minor, given here in German translation as Der Landjunker. Written in 1782, the play effectively invented Russian social comedy. Mitrofanushka's doting, tyrannical mother raises him into perfect uselessness while lecturing everyone on virtue.

Fonvizin aims his satire at the ignorant gentry of Catherine's age: brutal to serfs, proud of empty titles, hostile to learning. Honest officials and a wise uncle supply the standard the household fails. Humane as well as sharp, the comedy is still performed in Russia today. Its schoolroom scenes remain painfully funny anywhere exams are dodged. The German version opens Russia's first great play to new readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIALabor_CIA_La:
William Greider reported for the Washington Post on a quiet change in the labor movement's Cold War. After the CIA pulled out of funding overseas labor work, its exposure in 1967 having made the arrangement untenable, the AFL-CIO turned to subsidies from the Agency for International Development.

For two decades the CIA had channeled money to American unions fighting Communist labor federations abroad, and the pullout left the programs hunting for a new patron. AID money was overt, which changed both the politics and the paperwork. Greider's article records the handover as it happened, a small marker of the post-exposure cleanup.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIUSRecordingC:

The report also covers certain other matters pertaining to the Bureau. It is an internal reckoning made public: the department examining a private company's tie to its own police force.

A recording company linked to the FBI raises obvious questions about surveillance work and who performed it. The department's report was the official effort to answer them. Readers get the findings in the government's own words, from a period when the Bureau's practices faced hard public scrutiny.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FordGeraldRPort:

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Tru:
Mar-a-Lago, President Donald Trump's Florida resort, hosted official business while also operating as a private club. Lists of its visitors would show who gained access to the president there. This posting reports that the White House refused to keep or release such lists, citing ProPublica reporting.

Visitor logs matter because access is influence. Earlier administrations released White House logs as a transparency practice. govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran-nuc:
From the late 1940s into the early 1960s, the United States and Britain planned for a Soviet invasion of the Middle East. Part of that planning was denial: disabling or destroying the region's oil facilities before the Soviets could take them. This briefing book, posted in June 2016, publishes recently discovered British documents.

The documents give a new account of the CIA's role in the top-secret plan to ravage the Middle East oil industry. Scorched-earth planning against allied oil fields sounds extreme, yet it sat in official files for years. The record shows how completely Cold War planners subordinated the world economy to a single feared invasion.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iraq-nuc:
On June 7, 1981, Israeli jets attacked Iraq's Osirak nuclear research reactor at Tuwaitha and partially destroyed it. Joyce Battle edited this briefing book, posted exactly forty years later in June 2021. The aircraft and much of the equipment were American supplied, a fact the documents explore.

The posting's question has divided analysts ever since: was the strike a setback for Saddam Hussein's bomb program, or an impetus that drove it deeper underground? Declassified records let readers weigh both readings against what officials knew then. Few single air strikes have carried forty years of argument, which makes the file unusually instructive.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
Seventy-five years after Hiroshima and Nagasaki opened the atomic era, this briefing book, posted in May 2020, surveys American nuclear forces during the Cold War. Its themes are overkill and assured destruction: arsenals built far beyond any plausible military need.

The posting frames the hard questions that still follow the weapons. Their value, danger, and morality challenge politicians, strategists, and ordinary citizens alike. A survey built on the documentary record gives those debates a factual spine. Readers can see how the arsenal grew, what its builders said it was for, and why alternatives kept being searched for and not found.

In 1978 and 1979 American officials discovered the scale of Pakistan's secret nuclear program, and it posed what they called an acute dilemma. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 773, published in August 2021. New documents center on A. Q. Khan, the program's central figure.

Khan led shopping expeditions abroad for nuclear supplies, buying the parts of a bomb piece by piece. Officials even discussed the brutal possibility that some other country might destroy Pakistan's nuclear plants. The dilemma was real: punish an ally and push it closer to the bomb, or tolerate a program Washington publicly opposed. The papers show both horns of it.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia-intelligence:
In April 2018, the National Security Archive sued the CIA in federal court in Washington under the Freedom of Information Act. The suit sought twelve specific cables from November and December 2002, written or approved by Gina Haspel. She had just become the agency's acting director and was awaiting confirmation as its permanent head.

Those cables came from the Thailand black site Haspel ran, where prisoners were waterboarded and held in secret. Supporters said her record showed experience; critics said the cables would show exactly what she authorized. The Archive's suit is a case study in disclosure law used at a confirmation moment. That is when the public's need to know and the agency's wish for secrecy collide hardest. The posting lays out the filing and what each side wanted.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_2nd_Circuit_:
Who visits the White House is a basic record of who has the president's ear, and the Obama administration published about six million such visitor records. A National Security Archive news post from May 2020 reports a Second Circuit ruling in Doyle v. DHS that helped the White House keep later visitor logs secret, in a defeat for the groups that sued.

The Archive notes, with some bite, that the ruling never mentions Obama's six million released records at all. The case, brought with CREW and the Knight Institute, exposed how weak federal records laws can be when an administration simply refuses disclosure. For readers, the posting is both a case report and an argument: transparency that depends on a president's goodwill can vanish the moment goodwill does.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Breaking_New: On July 27, 2018, the National Security Archive reported a court ruling in its running fight over White House visitor logs.
